case: A 57-year-old female without any medical history was admitted for evaluation of a left ventricular tumor that was discovered incidentally. The patient was asymptomatic and had no relevant past medical history. Physical examination findings were not specifically described in the case report.

Left ventricular myxoma.description: A benign primary cardiac tumor, most commonly arising in the atria but rarely in the left ventricle; can be asymptomatic and found incidentally or cause obstruction/embolization.

Papillary fibroelastoma (left-sided/valv.description: A small, benign, frond-like tumor usually arising from cardiac valves (often aortic or mitral) and sometimes extending into the left ventricle; frequently detected incidentally but carries embolic risk.

Cardiac lipoma (left ventricular).description: A benign tumor composed of mature adipose tissue that can occur in the myocardium or endocardium; often asymptomatic and incidentally detected.

Cardiac fibroma (left ventricular).description: A benign fibrous tumor typically occurring in the ventricular myocardium; more common in children but can present in adults and may be incidental.

Left ventricular thrombus (pseudotumor).description: An intracavitary blood clot that can mimic a tumor on imaging; usually associated with prior myocardial infarction or cardiomyopathy but occasionally identified incidentally.

Metastatic cardiac tumor to the left ven.normalized_text: Metastatic cardiac tumor to the left ventricle
Metastatic cardiac tumor to the left ven.description: Secondary involvement of the heart from a distant primary malignancy (e.g., melanoma, lung, breast); often silent and detected incidentally, though more common than primary cardiac malignancies.

Primary cardiac sarcoma (e.g., undiffere.normalized_text: Primary cardiac sarcoma (e.g., undifferentiated or angiosarcoma)
Primary cardiac sarcoma (e.g., undiffere.description: A rare malignant primary cardiac tumor that can involve ventricular structures; often symptomatic but may be discovered incidentally in early stages.

case: A previously healthy 10-year-old boy presented with left upper quadrant abdominal pain that worsened with deep breathing or lying down, accompanied by fever. He also complained of mild cough and whitish sputum. On physical examination, the child was irritable but there were no other remarkable findings. Laboratory data showed elevated C-reactive protein (8.65 mg/dL) without leukocytosis and other findings were unremarkable.

Left lower lobe community-acquired pneum.description: Infection of the left lower lung that can present in children with referred left upper quadrant abdominal pain due to diaphragmatic irritation, along with fever and respiratory symptoms.

Atypical pneumonia (e.g., Mycoplasma pne.description: Atypical bacterial infection often causing mild, persistent cough and systemic symptoms with less striking exam and lab findings; pleuritic pain can occur from associated pleuritis.

Viral pleuritis/viral pneumonia.description: Viral infection of the respiratory tract with inflammation of the pleura causing pleuritic chest or referred upper abdominal pain, low to moderate fever, and mild respiratory symptoms.

Splenic abscess.description: A rare infection of the spleen presenting with fever and left upper quadrant abdominal pain; typically occurs in the setting of bacteremia, immunosuppression, or hemoglobinopathies.

Acute pancreatitis.description: Inflammation of the pancreas, which can cause left upper quadrant or epigastric pain that worsens when supine and may be associated with systemic inflammatory markers.

case: A 38-year-old woman presented with a three-day history of fever, generalized myalgia and arthralgia, and the sensation of difficulty when breathing in. She had poorly localized discomfort in the left diaphragmatic region on deep inspiration and loose stools over the preceding three days. Three days before presentation she had returned from a three-week trip to Western Australia, and 18 months earlier she had traveled to Vietnam. On examination she appeared well but was febrile at 38.0°C and tachypnoeic at 22 breaths/min, with all other observations normal. Examination of all other systems was unremarkable. Blood tests showed severe neutrophilia (18.9 × 10⁹/L; reference range 2.0-8.1), raised C reactive protein (354 mg/L; reference value <10), and normal renal and liver biochemistry. Chest radiography and urinalysis were normal. Blood cultures taken at presentation were negative.

Q fever (Coxiella burnetii).description: A zoonotic infection acquired via inhalation of aerosols from infected animals; common in Australia. It often presents as an acute febrile illness with myalgia and can involve pneumonia or hepatitis; labs typically show elevated inflammatory markers and leukocytosis while chest imaging may be normal early.

Leptospirosis.description: A spirochetal zoonosis acquired through contact with water contaminated by animal urine. Presents with acute febrile illness, severe myalgia (often calves), headache, and gastrointestinal symptoms; pulmonary involvement and pleuritic pain can occur.

Rickettsial infection (e.g., murine typh.normalized_text: Rickettsial infection (e.g., murine typhus or spotted fever group)
Rickettsial infection (e.g., murine typh.description: Tick- or flea-borne rickettsial diseases endemic in parts of Australia can present as acute febrile illnesses with myalgia, headache, elevated CRP, and leukocytosis; rash and eschar are common but not universal.

Pulmonary embolism.description: Acute obstruction of the pulmonary arteries, often presenting with tachypnea and pleuritic chest pain; fever and elevated inflammatory markers can occur, especially with pulmonary infarction. Recent travel is a risk factor.

Viral pleuritis/pleurodynia (Coxsackie v.description: An acute viral illness causing inflammation of the pleura and chest wall muscles, leading to sharp pleuritic pain (Bornholm disease), often with fever and myalgia; gastrointestinal symptoms may occur.

Influenza-like illness.description: A viral respiratory infection characterized by fever, myalgia, arthralgia, and systemic symptoms; gastrointestinal symptoms can occur. Early imaging is often normal.

Acute bacterial gastroenteritis with sys.normalized_text: Acute bacterial gastroenteritis with systemic inflammatory response
Acute bacterial gastroenteritis with sys.description: Enteric infections such as non-typhoidal Salmonella or Campylobacter can cause fever, diarrhea, and systemic inflammation; bacteremia can occur, though blood cultures may be negative.

case: A 60-year-old white Caucasian woman presented with a 4-year history of worsening gait and sensory disturbance accompanied by urinary urgency and nocturia. She reported slow deterioration in vision from age 50, though she could still drive. Her mother was registered blind and had Parkinson's disease with dementia. On examination, she had a spastic gait with normal power in lower limbs but increased tone and sustained ankle clonus. Reflexes were brisk with flexor plantar responses. She had mild reduction in visual acuity and dyschromatopsia, but no detectable visual field defect and preserved pupillary light reflexes. CSF analysis showed presence of oligoclonal bands. Routine hematological, biochemical and immunological blood tests were normal, including folate and vitamin B12. Anti-aquaporin 4 antibodies were negative in serum.

Primary progressive multiple sclerosis (.description: A form of multiple sclerosis characterized by a gradual progression of neurological disability from onset, often presenting with spastic paraparesis, sensory symptoms, and bladder dysfunction. CSF oligoclonal bands are common.

Hereditary spastic paraplegia (HSP), com.normalized_text: Hereditary spastic paraplegia (HSP), complex form with optic involvement (e.g., SPG7/OPA1-related)
Hereditary spastic paraplegia (HSP), com.description: A group of genetic disorders causing progressive upper motor neuron–predominant spasticity and gait disturbance; complex forms can include sensory symptoms, urinary urgency, and optic atrophy/dyschromatopsia.

Cervical spondylotic myelopathy.description: Degenerative cervical spine disease causing chronic compression of the spinal cord, leading to upper motor neuron signs in the legs (spastic gait, hyperreflexia, clonus), sensory disturbance, and urinary urgency.

Leber hereditary optic neuropathy with m.normalized_text: Leber hereditary optic neuropathy with multiple sclerosis–like demyelination (LHON-MS, Harding disease)
Leber hereditary optic neuropathy with m.description: A mitochondrial optic neuropathy that can coexist with an MS-like demyelinating syndrome, particularly in women; may show CSF oligoclonal bands and spinal cord/brain involvement.

Myelin oligodendrocyte glycoprotein anti.description: An inflammatory demyelinating disorder characterized by optic neuritis and myelitis; can be AQP4-negative. Typically shows relapsing attacks and optic neuritis with dyschromatopsia.

case: A 14-year-old female patient presented with generalized pruritus accompanied by scleral icterus and petechiae/ecchymoses on the extremities for over 2 months. She had no fever, abdominal pain, or distension. Past medical history included amenorrhea, menstrual irregularities, and acne. She had been taking Chinese herbal medicines (specific components unknown) for approximately 9 months. Physical examination revealed clear consciousness, facial acne and pigmentation, mild scleral and mucocutaneous jaundice, soft abdomen without tenderness or rebound tenderness, and no lower extremity edema.

Drug-induced cholestatic hepatitis (from.normalized_text: Drug-induced cholestatic hepatitis (from Chinese herbal medicine)
Drug-induced cholestatic hepatitis (from.description: Liver injury with a cholestatic pattern caused by medications or supplements; many Chinese herbal products can cause cholestasis leading to pruritus and jaundice.

Anabolic steroid–induced cholestasis (ad.normalized_text: Anabolic steroid–induced cholestasis (adulterated or androgenic herbal products)
Anabolic steroid–induced cholestasis (ad.description: 17-α-alkylated androgens (sometimes present in supplements/herbal products) can cause severe intrahepatic cholestasis with pruritus and jaundice; they can also cause acne and menstrual disturbances.

Autoimmune hepatitis.description: Immune-mediated hepatic inflammation common in adolescent females; can cause jaundice and coagulation abnormalities; may be insidious without pain or fever.

Primary sclerosing cholangitis.description: Chronic inflammatory cholangiopathy of intra- and extrahepatic bile ducts; can present in adolescents with pruritus and jaundice and progress insidiously.

Viral hepatitis (e.g., hepatitis A, B, o.normalized_text: Viral hepatitis (e.g., hepatitis A, B, or E; less likely C)
Viral hepatitis (e.g., hepatitis A, B, o.description: Hepatotropic viral infection causing jaundice; can occasionally cause cholestatic features with pruritus, especially in prolonged cholestatic hepatitis A.

Wilson disease (hepatic presentation).description: Inherited copper metabolism disorder presenting in adolescence with hepatic dysfunction, jaundice, and coagulopathy; may cause menstrual irregularities.

Immune thrombocytopenia (ITP).description: Autoimmune platelet destruction leading to petechiae and ecchymoses in otherwise well-appearing patients; often without systemic illness.

case: 66-year-old man with a 2-day history of fever, lethargy, polyarticular arthralgias, and a painful rash. Past history included hypertension, poorly controlled type 2 diabetes, hypercholesterolemia, and biopsy-proven autoimmune hepatitis; azathioprine 75 mg had been started 10 days earlier. On examination, temperature was 38°C with bilateral tender knees and a patellar tap. Labs showed leukocytosis with neutrophilia, elevated CRP and ESR, slightly elevated rheumatoid factor, negative anti-CCP and other autoimmune serologies, normal renal function and urinalysis, normal chest radiograph, and noninflammatory synovial fluid without bacteria or crystals.

Azathioprine-induced hypersensitivity (s.description: A drug-induced immune complex–like reaction occurring 1–3 weeks after starting a medication such as azathioprine, characterized by fever, rash, and arthralgias, often with neutrophilia and elevated inflammatory markers. Synovial fluid may be noninflammatory.

Drug-induced Sweet syndrome (acute febri.normalized_text: Drug-induced Sweet syndrome (acute febrile neutrophilic dermatosis)
Drug-induced Sweet syndrome (acute febri.description: An acute neutrophilic dermatosis often triggered by drugs (including azathioprine) or systemic disease, presenting with fever, painful erythematous plaques or nodules, neutrophilia, and arthralgias.

Parvovirus B19 infection (acute viral ar.description: Viral infection that in adults often presents with acute symmetric polyarthralgia and rash; RF can be transiently positive and anti-CCP negative. Synovial fluid may be noninflammatory.

Drug-induced leukocytoclastic vasculitis.description: Small-vessel immune complex vasculitis often triggered by medications, presenting with palpable purpura or painful rash, fever, and arthralgias; may occur 1–3 weeks after drug initiation.

Disseminated gonococcal infection (DGI).description: Systemic spread of Neisseria gonorrhoeae presenting with fever, migratory polyarthralgia, and a characteristic pustular or vesiculopustular rash; may progress to septic arthritis.

Adult-onset Still's disease.description: An autoinflammatory disorder with quotidian fevers, an evanescent salmon-colored rash, arthritis/arthralgia, neutrophilia, and high inflammatory markers; RF and anti-CCP are usually negative.

case: A 60-year-old woman presented after sustaining direct trauma to the anterior neck from a fall. She developed progressively worsening hoarse voice, difficulty swallowing, and pain with neck movement. Physical examination revealed visible neck swelling with bruising tracking onto the anterior chest wall. There was no tenderness on palpation of the cervical spine. On flexible nasal endoscopy, swelling of the posterior pharyngeal wall was observed, indicating potential airway compromise.

Thyroid cartilage (laryngeal) fracture.description: A fracture of the laryngeal framework, often from blunt anterior neck trauma, leading to airway compromise, dysphonia, and soft tissue swelling/hematoma.

Retropharyngeal hematoma.description: Bleeding into the retropharyngeal space after trauma, which can cause posterior pharyngeal wall bulging, dysphagia, and airway compromise.

Cervical tracheal injury (laryngotrachea.description: Traumatic injury to the cervical trachea or laryngotracheal junction causing airway instability, subcutaneous bleeding/air, and voice changes.

Arytenoid cartilage dislocation/subluxat.description: Displacement of the arytenoid cartilage often after blunt laryngeal trauma, leading to persistent dysphonia due to impaired vocal fold movement.

Cervical esophageal injury/perforation.description: Traumatic tear of the cervical esophagus leading to neck hematoma, posterior pharyngeal wall bulge, dysphagia, and potential mediastinal extension.

Expanding anterior neck hematoma (thyroi.normalized_text: Expanding anterior neck hematoma (thyroid or vascular injury)
Expanding anterior neck hematoma (thyroi.description: Bleeding from thyroid or neck vessels after blunt trauma causing a rapidly enlarging hematoma that can compress the airway and surrounding structures.

case: 37-year-old man with 3 months of weakness, irritability, poor concentration, cravings for sweets, and recurrent episodes of fogginess, confusion, cold clammy feeling, fatigue, and memory loss, often after several hours without eating, especially at night or early morning. He gained 30 lb during this period from drinking large amounts of cola for symptom relief. Symptoms recurred despite prior hospital evaluation several days earlier. Past history included umbilical hernia repair and back surgery 10 years earlier; no regular medications, no tobacco or illicit drug use, social alcohol use, and family history of diabetes without known personal diabetes. On examination he was confused, cold, and clammy; other physical findings were unremarkable. Routine labs, HbA1c, adrenal testing, calcium, PTH, thyroid tests, and gonadotropins were normal except mildly elevated prolactin. Imaging showed a 1.8 × 1.3 cm hypervascular slightly exophytic lesion arising anteriorly between the pancreatic head and neck.

Insulinoma (pancreatic beta-cell neuroen.description: A functional pancreatic neuroendocrine tumor that secretes insulin autonomously, causing recurrent fasting hypoglycemia with neuroglycopenic and adrenergic symptoms; typically small and hypervascular on imaging.

Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia type 1 (MEN.normalized_text: Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia type 1 (MEN1) with insulinoma
Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia type 1 (MEN.description: An inherited syndrome characterized by tumors of the parathyroid, pancreatic islet cells, and anterior pituitary. Patients may present with insulinoma-related hypoglycemia and pituitary hypersecretion (e.g., prolactin).

Noninsulinoma pancreatogenous hypoglycem.description: A condition of diffuse islet cell hyperplasia or dysregulated insulin secretion causing hypoglycemia, often postprandial; in adults it is frequently associated with prior gastric surgery but can occur idiopathically.

Factitious hypoglycemia (exogenous insul.normalized_text: Factitious hypoglycemia (exogenous insulin or sulfonylurea use)
Factitious hypoglycemia (exogenous insul.description: Surreptitious use of insulin or insulin secretagogues causing hypoglycemia; typically seen in individuals with access to these medications and characterized by recurrent episodes.

Reactive (postprandial) hypoglycemia.description: Hypoglycemia occurring within a few hours after meals due to excessive insulin response; often idiopathic or associated with prior gastric surgery or prediabetes.

case: A 39-year-old male, with no prior relevant medical history, presents with atraumatic intermittent sharp pain in the lower segment of the right anterior thoracic wall. The symptoms began two months earlier when the patient started exercising (CrossFit), mostly triggered by training (especially abdominal crunches) whilst being asymptomatic in normal daily activities.

Intercostal muscle strain.description: Overuse or microtears of the intercostal muscles from repetitive trunk flexion/rotation or heavy exertion, causing localized chest wall pain that worsens with movement.

Costochondritis.description: Inflammation of the costochondral or chondrosternal joints causing anterior chest wall pain, typically worsened by movement and physical activity.

Slipping rib syndrome (costal cartilage.normalized_text: Slipping rib syndrome (costal cartilage hypermobility of ribs 8–10)
Slipping rib syndrome (costal cartilage.description: Hypermobility of the anterior ends of the lower ribs (often 8–10) leads to irritation of intercostal nerves and ligaments, causing sharp, activity-related pain in the lower anterior or lateral chest.

Rectus abdominis insertional tendinopath.description: Overuse injury of the rectus abdominis muscle or its tendinous insertions on the costal cartilages, producing pain with abdominal flexion exercises.

Rib stress fracture.description: Repetitive loading from activities like rowing or high-intensity training can cause microfractures in ribs, leading to localized chest wall pain that worsens with exertion.

Intercostal neuralgia.description: Irritation or entrapment of an intercostal nerve causing sharp, shooting pain along the chest wall, often aggravated by movement.

case: A 31-year-old woman underwent barium enema examination as part of a medical checkup. She had been healthy without specific complaints and had no significant past medical or family history. The patient was 161 cm in height and weighed 44 kg, appeared well, and the physical examination showed no abnormalities. Complete blood cell count and biochemical analysis of the blood for hepatic and renal function, urine analysis, and fecal occult blood test were all within normal limits. The tumor markers for CEA and CA 19-9 were also normal. No lesions were observed on the upper endoscopy and the abdominal ultrasound.

Colonic diverticulosis.description: Outpouchings of the colonic mucosa and submucosa, most often in the sigmoid colon; frequently discovered incidentally and usually asymptomatic.

Colorectal adenomatous polyps.description: Benign neoplastic polyps that can be precursors to colorectal cancer; commonly asymptomatic and discovered on screening.

Early-stage colorectal cancer.description: Malignant tumor of the colon or rectum; early disease can be asymptomatic and detected only through screening.

Dolichocolon (redundant colon).description: An anatomic variant characterized by an abnormally long colon with additional loops; often incidental and asymptomatic, sometimes associated with constipation.

Intestinal malrotation (adult, incidenta.description: Congenital anomaly of midgut rotation that may persist into adulthood and be found incidentally on imaging; many adults remain asymptomatic.

case: A 67-year-old previously healthy male presented with a 4-month history of dry cough, wheezing, and mild dyspnea that had initially been diagnosed as eosinophilic asthma at another hospital, with symptoms worsening despite treatment with inhaled bronchodilators and corticosteroids. He had no smoking history and unremarkable medical history. On examination, he required 1L nasal cannula oxygen with SaO2 of 96%, had decreased breath sounds in the right lower lung field with fine crackles, and no raised JVP, murmurs, gallop, or peripheral edema. Chest x-ray showed right ground glass opacities, and high-resolution CT revealed ground glass opacities surrounded by consolidation in the right lower lung field.

Cryptogenic organizing pneumonia (COP).description: A noninfectious inflammatory lung disease characterized by intra-alveolar granulation tissue (organizing pneumonia). It presents subacutely with cough and dyspnea and often shows patchy consolidation or ground-glass opacities; the reversed halo (atoll) sign on HRCT is suggestive.

Chronic eosinophilic pneumonia (CEP).description: An eosinophilic lung disease often associated with asthma, presenting with subacute cough, dyspnea, and peripheral blood or alveolar eosinophilia. Imaging typically shows peripheral, often upper-lobe predominant ground-glass or consolidative opacities.

Hypersensitivity pneumonitis (HP).description: An immune-mediated interstitial lung disease caused by inhaled antigens (e.g., molds, birds), presenting with cough and dyspnea; HRCT often shows diffuse ground-glass opacities, mosaic attenuation, and air-trapping.

Aspiration pneumonia/aspiration pneumoni.description: Inflammation or infection from aspiration of oropharyngeal/gastric contents, often involving dependent lung segments such as the right lower lobe; imaging can show ground-glass opacities and consolidation.

Lung adenocarcinoma with lepidic growth.normalized_text: Lung adenocarcinoma with lepidic growth (invasive mucinous adenocarcinoma)
Lung adenocarcinoma with lepidic growth.description: A form of adenocarcinoma that spreads along alveolar structures (lepidic pattern), commonly presenting with chronic cough and non-resolving ground-glass or consolidative opacities, often unilateral.

Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (PJP).description: An opportunistic fungal pneumonia typically seen in immunocompromised patients, presenting with subacute dry cough, dyspnea, and hypoxemia; imaging often shows bilateral ground-glass opacities.

case: A 12-year-old boy presented with a 1-month history of malaise, fevers, abdominal pain, and worsening pallor. His symptoms began with headache and abdominal pain, with an initial temperature of 38.6°C and pale skin. He experienced persistent upper abdominal pain and recurrent fevers. The patient reported nausea, occasional diarrhea, headache, myalgias, fatigue, and occasional dizziness. He described nearly constant periumbilical pain radiating to the left lower quadrant, with occasional blood in stools. His height was 132 cm (1st percentile), weight 26.8 kg (1st percentile), with recent 1 kg weight loss. Physical examination revealed pale skin and mucosa, distended abdomen with mild tenderness in right upper and left lower quadrants, and ecchymoses on the shins. He had visited the Dominican Republic 3 months prior. Laboratory tests showed severe microcytic anemia (hemoglobin 6.7 g/dL), elevated inflammatory markers (ESR >140 mm/hr, CRP 143.2 mg/liter), and elevated ferritin (320 μg/L).

diagnoses.name: Mixed-cellularity subtype of classic Hodgkin's lymphoma
diagnoses.normalized_text: Mixed-cellularity subtype of classic Hodgkin's lymphoma

Crohn disease (inflammatory bowel diseas.description: A chronic, transmural inflammatory disease of the gastrointestinal tract that often presents in adolescents with abdominal pain, diarrhea, weight loss, growth delay, and anemia due to chronic inflammation and blood loss.

Ulcerative colitis.description: A chronic inflammatory disease limited to the colon and rectum, characterized by mucosal inflammation causing bloody diarrhea, abdominal pain, and systemic symptoms.

Acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL).description: A malignant proliferation of lymphoid precursors in bone marrow, common in children, presenting with anemia, infections/fevers, bleeding/bruising, bone pain, and organomegaly.

Enteric (typhoid) fever.description: Systemic infection by Salmonella enterica serovar Typhi or Paratyphi, causing prolonged fever, abdominal pain, headache, and gastrointestinal symptoms after travel to endemic areas.

Hookworm infection (Ancylostoma duodenal.description: Intestinal helminth infection acquired in tropical regions causing chronic intestinal blood loss, iron deficiency anemia, and gastrointestinal symptoms.

Celiac disease.description: An autoimmune enteropathy triggered by gluten, leading to villous atrophy, malabsorption, iron deficiency anemia, growth failure, and gastrointestinal symptoms.

case: A 39-year-old man presented to the emergency department during the summer with a 4-day history of fever with shaking chills, diffuse headache, and fatigue following his return from a 2-week trip to East Africa. During his trip to Tanzania, he had been on safari without animal contact but received mosquito bites, especially during the first days. He consumed cooked shrimp and lobster and a small amount of raw tuna. On the second-to-last day of the trip, he developed nausea, vomiting, and nonbloody diarrhea. Upon returning to Massachusetts, he experienced fever (38.3°C to 39.5°C), shaking chills, diffuse headache, and lower back pain. He reported weakness, anorexia, decreased urine output with dark urine, and blurry vision during fever episodes. His medical history included degenerative knee disease with previous glucocorticoid injections. On examination, he had a temperature of 38.9°C, blood pressure 113/62 mm Hg, facial flushing, mild scleral icterus, and dark brown urine.

Plasmodium falciparum malaria.description: A severe, potentially life-threatening parasitic infection transmitted by Anopheles mosquitoes, common in sub-Saharan Africa; characterized by high fevers, hemolysis, and possible acute kidney injury.

Leptospirosis (Weil disease).description: A zoonotic spirochetal infection often acquired via exposure to water contaminated with animal urine; severe forms (Weil disease) cause jaundice, renal failure, and hemorrhage.

Yellow fever.description: A mosquito-borne flavivirus endemic in parts of Africa that can cause abrupt fever, headache, severe back pain, jaundice, and renal failure.

Dengue fever.description: A mosquito-borne viral illness causing acute febrile illness with severe headache, myalgias/arthralgias, and sometimes rash; severe cases can cause plasma leakage and hemorrhage.

Enteric (typhoid) fever due to Salmonell.normalized_text: Enteric (typhoid) fever due to Salmonella enterica serotype Typhi/Paratyphi
Enteric (typhoid) fever due to Salmonell.description: A systemic bacterial infection acquired via contaminated food or water, causing sustained fever, abdominal symptoms, and bacteremia.

Acute viral hepatitis (A or E).description: Acute hepatitis A or E can be acquired via fecal-oral route; HAV often linked to contaminated food including shellfish, HEV prevalent in developing regions; presents with jaundice, dark urine, and systemic symptoms.

Acute hemolysis due to G6PD deficiency (.normalized_text: Acute hemolysis due to G6PD deficiency (triggered by infection)
Acute hemolysis due to G6PD deficiency (.description: An X-linked enzymatic defect causing red blood cells to hemolyze under oxidative stress; infections can precipitate acute hemolysis with jaundice and dark urine.

case: 24-year-old male with quadriplegia from a car accident 5 years prior that required cervical spine stabilization with metal plates. Presented with dysphagia, odynophagia, neck pain, fever, and chills. Medical history significant for quadriplegia requiring cervical spine stabilization with metal plates. CT and MRI showed large paraspinal abscess extending from cervical spine 4 to thoracic spine 11.

Infected cervical spinal instrumentation.normalized_text: Infected cervical spinal instrumentation with paraspinal abscess
Infected cervical spinal instrumentation.description: Late-onset infection of spinal hardware due to biofilm formation can lead to contiguous spread and formation of large prevertebral/paraspinal abscesses, particularly in the cervical region, causing compressive symptoms and systemic infection.

Spinal epidural abscess (cervicothoracic.description: A collection of pus in the epidural space, often due to hematogenous spread or contiguous infection, presenting with fever and back/neck pain and carrying a high risk of neurologic compromise; may coexist with or arise from paraspinal/prevertebral abscesses.

Vertebral osteomyelitis/discitis (cervic.normalized_text: Vertebral osteomyelitis/discitis (cervicothoracic) with associated paraspinal abscess
Vertebral osteomyelitis/discitis (cervic.description: Infection of the vertebral bodies and intervertebral discs that can progress to form paraspinal or prevertebral abscesses; commonly caused by Staphylococcus aureus via hematogenous seeding or contiguous spread.

Retropharyngeal abscess with descending.description: Deep neck space infection in the retropharyngeal space that can cause dysphagia, odynophagia, and neck pain, and may descend into the mediastinum or prevertebral/paraspinal spaces, especially in severe or untreated cases.

Tuberculous spondylitis (Pott disease) w.normalized_text: Tuberculous spondylitis (Pott disease) with paraspinal 'cold' abscess
Tuberculous spondylitis (Pott disease) w.description: Mycobacterial infection of the spine causing chronic vertebral destruction and large paraspinal 'cold' abscesses; typically presents subacutely with back/neck pain and constitutional symptoms.

case: A 58-year-old male with worsening nausea for the past 72 hours presented to the emergency department with severe chest pain radiating to the back in the context of 4 recent episodes of non-bloody, non-bilious emesis. He was afebrile, diaphoretic, and mildly tachycardic. Cardiac workup, complete blood count, and electrolytes were normal.

Acute aortic dissection.description: A tear in the intimal layer of the aorta allowing blood to dissect the vessel wall, causing sudden severe chest or back pain and autonomic symptoms.

Esophageal rupture (Boerhaave syndrome).description: Full-thickness tear of the esophagus, often after forceful vomiting, leading to severe chest pain and mediastinal contamination.

Acute pancreatitis.description: Inflammation of the pancreas, typically causing severe epigastric pain radiating to the back with nausea and vomiting.

Pulmonary embolism.description: Obstruction of pulmonary arteries by thrombus causing acute chest pain, tachycardia, and autonomic symptoms; cardiac biomarkers may be normal.

Diffuse esophageal spasm (noncardiac eso.normalized_text: Diffuse esophageal spasm (noncardiac esophageal chest pain)
Diffuse esophageal spasm (noncardiac eso.description: Disordered esophageal motility causing intermittent severe chest pain that can mimic cardiac pain and sometimes radiates to the back.

case: 27-year-old man with 2-year history of recurrent convulsions. Episodes began with shaking of the trunk, arms, and legs lasting 4–5 minutes, sometimes preceded by occipital pain radiating to the neck, blurred vision, palpitations, nausea, and difficulty concentrating. Four months before admission, he had an event with sudden stiffening, fall backward, shaking for 5–8 minutes, and urinary incontinence. Seizure frequency increased to about weekly despite levetiracetam, with another witnessed episode 1 month before admission lasting about 2 minutes. On examination, he was awake and alert but mute, with a stiff posture and intermittent nonrhythmic tremulous movements of the trunk and limbs. He had extensive burn scars on the face, trunk, back, arms, and legs. History included febrile seizure in childhood, multiple concussions, asthma, major depressive disorder, chronic PTSD, and panic disorder with agoraphobia. Laboratory studies were largely normal except for mildly elevated lactate and creatine kinase.

Psychogenic nonepileptic seizures (PNES).description: Paroxysmal events resembling epileptic seizures without abnormal cortical discharges, often related to psychological factors such as trauma, PTSD, anxiety, or depression.

Generalized tonic–clonic epilepsy.description: Epileptic disorder characterized by generalized tonic stiffening followed by clonic jerking, often with loss of consciousness and postictal confusion.

Occipital lobe epilepsy with secondary g.normalized_text: Occipital lobe epilepsy with secondary generalization
Occipital lobe epilepsy with secondary g.description: Focal epilepsy originating in the occipital cortex, often presenting with visual symptoms or occipital headache that may secondarily generalize to tonic–clonic seizures.

Frontal lobe epilepsy (hypermotor/tonic.description: Focal seizures arising from the frontal lobes that often have abrupt onset with tonic posturing, hypermotor behaviors, and can generalize; episodes are typically brief and may occur in clusters.

Convulsive syncope due to cardiac arrhyt.normalized_text: Convulsive syncope due to cardiac arrhythmia
Convulsive syncope due to cardiac arrhyt.description: Transient loss of consciousness from cerebral hypoperfusion that can include myoclonic or tonic movements; often preceded by palpitations or autonomic symptoms.

Migraine with brainstem/occipital aura w.normalized_text: Migraine with brainstem/occipital aura with seizure trigger (migralepsy)
Migraine with brainstem/occipital aura w.description: Rare phenomenon where a seizure occurs during or within an hour after a migraine aura, often with visual or occipital symptoms and nausea.

case: 92-year-old woman with BMI 14.2 kg/m². Past history: no abdominal surgery, five children by normal vaginal delivery. Presenting with: 2-day history of sudden onset right knee pain, 1-day history of nausea and vomiting. Physical exam: no knee swelling/tenderness, patient frequently flexed right knee for pain relief, abdominal distension present, tenderness to deep palpation but no peritoneal irritation signs, no abdominal mass. Rectal exam revealed small extraluminal mass on right side. Initial abdominal radiograph showed small-bowel obstruction.

Obturator hernia causing small-bowel obs.normalized_text: Obturator hernia causing small-bowel obstruction (Howship–Romberg syndrome)
Obturator hernia causing small-bowel obs.description: A rare pelvic hernia in which bowel herniates through the obturator canal, classically in thin, elderly, multiparous women. It often presents with small-bowel obstruction and medial thigh or knee pain from obturator nerve compression, relieved by hip flexion.

Incarcerated femoral hernia with small-b.normalized_text: Incarcerated femoral hernia with small-bowel obstruction
Incarcerated femoral hernia with small-b.description: Herniation below the inguinal ligament through the femoral canal, common in elderly, thin, multiparous women and prone to incarceration causing small-bowel obstruction.

Gallstone ileus.description: Mechanical small-bowel obstruction caused by a gallstone that has passed through a biliary-enteric fistula, typically affecting elderly women.

Small-bowel neoplasm causing obstruction.normalized_text: Small-bowel neoplasm causing obstruction (e.g., primary tumor or metastatic lesion)
Small-bowel neoplasm causing obstruction.description: Intraluminal or mural tumor (primary or metastatic) causing mechanical small-bowel obstruction; more common in older adults and may present with weight loss and obstruction.

Adhesive small-bowel obstruction (ASBO).normalized_text: Adhesive small-bowel obstruction (ASBO) without prior surgery (congenital/idiopathic adhesions)
Adhesive small-bowel obstruction (ASBO).description: Mechanical obstruction due to intra-abdominal adhesions; most commonly follows prior surgery, but can rarely occur from congenital or inflammatory adhesions.

case: 23-year-old Korean female with 6 months of recurrent bilateral visual field defects and headache, worsening 1 month before presentation. She presented with 1 day of left-eye visual disturbance/field defect, then developed sudden left-sided hearing loss 2 days later. Three weeks after initial presentation, she had new right-eye visual field defect, followed 2 days later by tinnitus, severe headache, and arm numbness. She denied significant past medical history, medication use, or pregnancy. On examination, pupils were reactive without RAPD; visual acuity was 20/20 right and 20/25 left, IOP was 18 mmHg bilaterally, and anterior segments were normal. Laboratory studies were unremarkable, and CSF showed mildly elevated protein (74.4 mg/dL) without oligoclonal bands.

Susac syndrome (retino-cochleo-cerebral.description: An autoimmune microangiopathy affecting precapillary arterioles of the brain, retina, and inner ear, causing branch retinal artery occlusions, sensorineural hearing loss, and encephalopathy/headache in young women.

Multiple sclerosis.description: A relapsing inflammatory demyelinating disease of the CNS that can cause optic neuritis and multifocal neurologic deficits.

Neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder (.description: An autoimmune astrocytopathy characterized by severe optic neuritis and longitudinally extensive myelitis; can present with relapses affecting optic nerves and brainstem.

MOG antibody-associated disease (MOGAD).description: An inflammatory demyelinating disorder often causing recurrent bilateral optic neuritis, sometimes with headache and myelitis; distinct from MS and NMOSD.

Migraine with aura (including possible v.normalized_text: Migraine with aura (including possible vestibular/cochlear migraine)
Migraine with aura (including possible v.description: A primary headache disorder with transient neurologic auras (visual and sensory); some patients experience vestibular symptoms and tinnitus.

Primary angiitis of the central nervous.normalized_text: Primary angiitis of the central nervous system (PACNS)
Primary angiitis of the central nervous.description: A rare vasculitis confined to the CNS causing headaches and multifocal neurologic deficits; CSF often shows inflammatory changes.

case: A 73-year-old woman with a 10-year history of severe paraspinal muscle atrophy and cerebellar ataxia. Symptoms began at age 63 with slight stooping posture, then progressed to gait instability requiring a walking stick by age 68 and difficulty climbing stairs by age 70. Exam showed moderate neck flexion weakness, mild proximal limb weakness, poor tandem gait balance without limb ataxia, and MMSE 25. Labs: elevated creatine kinase, normal blood and CSF lactate, slightly low TSH, elevated antithyroglobulin and antithyroid peroxidase antibodies, elevated rheumatoid factor, and mild ANA positivity. EMG showed mild myopathic features. Audiometry showed sensorineural high-frequency hearing loss, and Holter monitoring showed frequent premature contractions.

Myofibrillar myopathy (e.g., desmin- or.normalized_text: Myofibrillar myopathy (e.g., desmin- or filamin C–related)
Myofibrillar myopathy (e.g., desmin- or.description: A group of adult-onset genetic myopathies characterized by disintegration of myofibrils and accumulation of protein aggregates, often with prominent axial and proximal weakness, paraspinal muscle atrophy, and potential cardiac conduction abnormalities; some subtypes may include sensorineural hearing loss.

Late-onset Pompe disease (acid maltase d.description: A metabolic myopathy due to lysosomal acid alpha-glucosidase deficiency, typically presenting in adulthood with axial and proximal muscle weakness, paraspinal/neck flexor involvement, and elevated CK; respiratory muscle weakness is common, cardiac involvement is less marked in adults.

Sporadic inclusion body myositis (sIBM).description: The most common inflammatory myopathy in older adults, with slowly progressive muscle weakness often involving quadriceps, finger flexors, and sometimes axial muscles; CK is variably elevated and EMG shows myopathic features.

Mitochondrial myopathy with ataxia (e.g..normalized_text: Mitochondrial myopathy with ataxia (e.g., POLG-related disorder or late-onset mitochondrial syndrome)
Mitochondrial myopathy with ataxia (e.g..description: Mitochondrial disorders can present in late adulthood with multisystem involvement including myopathy, cerebellar ataxia, sensorineural hearing loss, and cardiac conduction abnormalities; CK can be elevated and EMG shows myopathic changes.

Autoimmune thyroid disease–associated my.normalized_text: Autoimmune thyroid disease–associated myopathy with autoimmune cerebellar ataxia (e.g., Hashimoto-related/anti-GAD spectrum)
Autoimmune thyroid disease–associated my.description: Autoimmune thyroid disease can be associated with inflammatory myopathy and autoimmune cerebellar ataxia; patients may have elevated anti-thyroid antibodies and other autoimmune markers; CK may be elevated and EMG myopathic.

case: A 2-year-old Korean male was admitted for evaluation and management of left hip pain. Physical examination revealed several palpable lymph nodes in the left inguinal area and an ill-defined heterogeneous mass-like lesion in the left anteromedial muscle. Peripheral blood examination showed hemoglobin 9.6 g/dL, white blood cell count 6.83 × 10^9/L, platelet count 182 × 10^9/L, and 5 atypical lymphocytes per 100 white blood cells. Immunophenotyping of neoplastic cells showed positivity for CD45 (99.0%), CD19 (94.84%), CD10 (27.64%), CD20 (94.24%), HLA-DR (95.70%), surface IgG lambda (96.45%), CD13 (22.46%), and CD117 (22.22%), and negativity for CD34 (0.01%), Tdt (0.64%), myeloperoxidase (0.01%), and various T-cell and myeloid markers.
