diagnoses.icd11_title: B-cell lymphoma unclassifiable with features intermediate between Burkitt lymphoma and diffuse large B-cell lymphoma

Burkitt lymphoma (mature B-cell lymphoma.description: An aggressive mature B-cell lymphoma of childhood characterized by rapidly growing extranodal masses, high proliferation, and surface immunoglobulin expression; typically CD19/20/10 positive, TdT negative.

Pediatric diffuse large B-cell lymphoma.description: A mature B-cell lymphoma presenting with nodal or extranodal masses in children; typically expresses CD19/CD20 and surface immunoglobulin; TdT negative.

B-lymphoblastic lymphoma/leukemia (B-ALL.description: A neoplasm of immature B-cell precursors typically presenting in young children with marrow/blood involvement or mass lesions; usually expresses TdT and/or CD34 and lacks strong surface immunoglobulin.

Pediatric-type follicular lymphoma.description: An indolent germinal center B-cell lymphoma occurring in children, often with localized nodal disease; typically CD10 positive, CD20 positive, and surface immunoglobulin positive; lacks TdT.

Rhabdomyosarcoma.description: A common pediatric soft tissue sarcoma arising from skeletal muscle lineage, often presenting with a painful mass and regional lymph node involvement.

case: A 12-year-old Malagasy boy consulted for a fever that had been evolving for two months, with a notion of trauma and pain in the right upper quadrant as well as chronic diarrhoea. A parasitological examination of the stool found eggs of Schistosoma mansoni. An ultrasound and a CT scan were then ordered.

Intestinal/hepatosplenic schistosomiasis.description: Chronic infection by S. mansoni causing intestinal inflammation (diarrhea, abdominal pain) and, with heavier burdens or chronicity, hepatosplenic involvement with hepatic inflammation/fibrosis leading to right upper quadrant pain and prolonged fever; common in endemic regions.

Amebic liver abscess (Entamoeba histolyt.description: An invasive complication of E. histolytica infection where trophozoites form an abscess in the liver, typically presenting with fever and right upper quadrant pain; may follow or accompany amebic colitis.

Pyogenic liver abscess.description: A bacterial infection of the liver parenchyma forming a pus-filled cavity, often due to biliary tract disease, portal venous seeding from enteric infections, or hematogenous spread; presents with fever and right upper quadrant pain.

Abdominal (gastrointestinal/hepatic) tub.description: Mycobacterial infection involving the intestines, mesenteric nodes, peritoneum, or liver, causing chronic constitutional symptoms and gastrointestinal complaints; can cause hepatomegaly and RUQ discomfort if hepatic involvement occurs.

Visceral leishmaniasis (kala-azar).description: A protozoal infection (Leishmania) transmitted by sandflies causing prolonged fever, hepatosplenomegaly, weight loss, and cytopenias; GI symptoms can occur, with abdominal pain from organ enlargement.

case: 44-year-old man with 1 month of intermittent substernal burning chest pain, now severe and radiating to the left arm, awakening him from sleep 1 hour prior to presentation, with nausea and nonbilious, nonbloody vomiting. Pain was nonexertional and temporarily relieved by antacids/omeprazole. He denied dyspnea, fever, cough, trauma, edema, or immobilization. Past medical history was unremarkable; he had a prior platelet count around 600,000/mm³ 12 years earlier and reported intermittent generalized pruritus after hot showers, without bleeding, thrombosis, neurologic symptoms, or erythromelalgia. Exam showed he was afebrile, in distress, with normal heart and lung findings, no JVD or edema, and nontender chest and abdomen. Labs: troponin 0.08 ng/mL, WBC 22,000/mm³ with neutrophilia and bandemia, platelets 771,000/mm³, hemoglobin 17.5 g/dL, fasting glucose 192 mg/dL.

diagnoses.name: ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction
diagnoses.icd11_title: Acute ST segment elevation myocardial infarction

Non–ST-elevation myocardial infarction (.description: Acute coronary syndrome due to partial coronary artery occlusion causing myocardial ischemia and necrosis with modest troponin elevation, often presenting with angina-like chest pain and autonomic symptoms.

Vasospastic (Prinzmetal) angina.description: Episodic coronary artery spasm causing transient myocardial ischemia, often occurring at rest or at night, sometimes with transient troponin elevation.

Gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD) w.normalized_text: Gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD) with possible erosive esophagitis
Gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD) w.description: Reflux of gastric contents into the esophagus causing mucosal irritation, presenting with burning substernal pain that can be nocturnal and relieved by acid suppression.

Esophageal spasm.description: Disordered esophageal motility causing episodic chest pain that can mimic angina and occasionally radiate, often triggered by cold liquids or stress.

Polycythemia vera (JAK2-positive myelopr.description: A clonal myeloproliferative disorder characterized by increased red cell mass and often elevated platelets and leukocytes; associated with aquagenic pruritus and high risk of thrombosis.

case: Newborn girl admitted to the NICU after cardiorespiratory arrest at delivery. Pregnancy was complicated by maternal hepatitis C infection, treated urogenital Chlamydia trachomatis infection, and gestational hypertension; prenatal ultrasounds showed right urinary tract dilation from 20 weeks to term. At 40 weeks, after prolonged labor with meconium-stained fluid, cesarean delivery was performed for nonreassuring fetal status and breech presentation. The infant was limp, apneic, and required 16 minutes of resuscitation with intubation, CPR, epinephrine, and saline boluses before return of spontaneous circulation. Apgar scores were 1, 0, 0, 1, and 3 at 1, 5, 10, 15, and 20 minutes. On NICU arrival, she was hypothermic (34.9°C) and mechanically ventilated; therapeutic hypothermia was started.

Hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy (HIE) du.normalized_text: Hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy (HIE) due to perinatal asphyxia
Hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy (HIE) du.description: Brain and systemic injury from inadequate oxygenation and perfusion around the time of birth; commonly presents with severe depression at birth and low Apgar scores, often managed with therapeutic hypothermia.

Meconium aspiration syndrome.description: Respiratory failure caused by aspiration of meconium-stained amniotic fluid, leading to airway obstruction, chemical pneumonitis, surfactant inactivation, and potential secondary pulmonary hypertension.

Persistent pulmonary hypertension of the.normalized_text: Persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn (PPHN)
Persistent pulmonary hypertension of the.description: Failure of normal circulatory transition after birth, with high pulmonary vascular resistance causing right-to-left shunting and severe hypoxemia; often triggered by conditions like meconium aspiration or perinatal asphyxia.

Early-onset neonatal sepsis.description: Systemic infection occurring within the first 72 hours of life, commonly due to Group B Streptococcus or E. coli; can present with respiratory distress, apnea, hypotonia, and cardiovascular instability.

Critical congenital heart disease (ducta.description: Structural heart defects (e.g., transposition of the great arteries, hypoplastic left heart, pulmonary or aortic atresia) that can cause profound hypoxemia or shock in the immediate neonatal period.

Neonatal intracranial hemorrhage or trau.normalized_text: Neonatal intracranial hemorrhage or traumatic birth injury
Neonatal intracranial hemorrhage or trau.description: Bleeding within the cranial vault or traumatic injury associated with difficult delivery, which can cause apnea, hypotonia, seizures, and hemodynamic instability.

case: 54-year-old man with a history of polysubstance abuse and treatment-naïve hepatitis C presented with altered mental status. He was afebrile, drowsy, hypertensive (172/110 mmHg), with distended jugular veins and bibasilar crackles. Labs showed severe renal failure (creatinine 16.0 mg/dL, BUN 99 mg/dL), mild anemia, proteinuria with urine protein-to-creatinine ratio 1.9, elevated LDH, rare schistocytes, and low C3 with normal C4. Urine toxicology was positive for cocaine and metabolites; blood and urine cultures were negative. Kidney ultrasound showed echogenic kidneys measuring 9.8 cm and 10.3 cm. Family history included a sister with renal failure requiring dialysis at age 45.

Atypical hemolytic uremic syndrome (aHUS.description: Complement-mediated thrombotic microangiopathy causing microangiopathic hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia (variable), and acute kidney injury; often associated with low C3 and can have familial predisposition due to complement regulatory gene defects.

Malignant hypertension with thrombotic m.description: Severe, abrupt hypertension leading to endothelial injury, arteriolar fibrinoid necrosis, and TMA, causing acute kidney injury, mild hemolysis, and end-organ damage.

C3 glomerulopathy (C3 glomerulonephritis.description: Complement dysregulation of the alternative pathway leading to predominant C3 deposition in glomeruli, presenting with hematuria/proteinuria and progressive renal dysfunction; often shows low C3 with normal C4 and can be familial.

Hepatitis C–associated mixed cryoglobuli.normalized_text: Hepatitis C–associated mixed cryoglobulinemic glomerulonephritis (MPGN pattern)
Hepatitis C–associated mixed cryoglobuli.description: Immune complex–mediated glomerulonephritis driven by HCV with cryoglobulin deposition, often presenting with proteinuria, hematuria, hypertension, and low complement (particularly low C4).

Cocaine/levamisole-associated ANCA vascu.description: ANCA-associated small-vessel vasculitis triggered by levamisole-adulterated cocaine, causing pauci-immune glomerulonephritis with rapidly progressive renal failure and systemic features (skin necrosis, ENT disease).

APOL1-associated focal segmental glomeru.normalized_text: APOL1-associated focal segmental glomerulosclerosis (FSGS) or hereditary CKD
APOL1-associated focal segmental glomeru.description: Genetic predisposition (e.g., APOL1 high-risk variants) can cause FSGS and progressive CKD, often presenting with proteinuria, hypertension, and progression to ESRD, sometimes clustering in families.

Infection-related (post-infectious) glom.description: Immune complex–mediated GN following infection (often streptococcal or staphylococcal), characterized by low C3 with normalizing over weeks, presenting with hematuria, proteinuria, hypertension, and renal dysfunction.

case: 44-year-old Chinese woman with no significant prior medical history presented with 7 weeks of progressively worsening nausea and vomiting with 13 kg weight loss. She denied abdominal pain, distension, or diarrhea. Initial treatment for presumed functional gastrointestinal disorder, including antidepressants, prokinetics, and anti-emetics, was ineffective. Eight days after admission, she developed metabolic alkalosis, acute respiratory failure, and neurological deficits. Examination showed right-sided limb paralysis, horizontal nystagmus, loss of pharyngeal reflex, decreased tendon reflexes on the right, and bilateral Babinski signs. Prior gastroscopy and abdominal CT were normal. Laboratory studies showed normal liver, kidney, thyroid, autoimmune, and glucose-related tests; serum AQP4-IgG was negative, but cerebrospinal fluid AQP4-IgG was positive.

Neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder (.normalized_text: Neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder (NMOSD) with area postrema syndrome and brainstem involvement
Neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder (.description: An autoimmune astrocytopathy commonly associated with AQP4-IgG antibodies, characterized by relapsing attacks affecting optic nerves, spinal cord, and brainstem. Area postrema involvement causes intractable nausea/vomiting; brainstem lesions can produce cranial nerve deficits and respiratory failure.

Multiple sclerosis (brainstem-predominan.description: A demyelinating disease of the CNS characterized by disseminated lesions in time and space. Brainstem involvement can cause cranial nerve signs, nystagmus, and long-tract signs.

Bickerstaff brainstem encephalitis (BBE).description: An immune-mediated brainstem encephalitis often associated with anti-GQ1b antibodies, characterized by ophthalmoplegia, ataxia, altered consciousness, and areflexia; overlaps with Miller Fisher/GBS spectrum.

Wernicke encephalopathy secondary to thi.normalized_text: Wernicke encephalopathy secondary to thiamine deficiency from prolonged vomiting
Wernicke encephalopathy secondary to thi.description: An acute neuropsychiatric syndrome due to thiamine deficiency, classically presenting with encephalopathy, oculomotor abnormalities, and gait ataxia; can be precipitated by malnutrition or prolonged vomiting.

Brainstem stroke (e.g., lateral medullar.normalized_text: Brainstem stroke (e.g., lateral medullary or pontine infarct)
Brainstem stroke (e.g., lateral medullar.description: Ischemic infarction of the brainstem can cause bulbar dysfunction, nystagmus, respiratory compromise, and long-tract signs. Lateral medullary (Wallenberg) syndrome often presents with dysphagia, nystagmus, and autonomic symptoms.

case: 47-year-old male with 2-month history of fever, headache, myalgia, arthralgia, and malaise. History of inguinal hernia repair surgery 10 years ago and cardiac disease. On admission, body temperature was 37.3°C. Physical examination revealed aortic valve diastolic murmurs at the precordium.

Subacute infective endocarditis (aortic.normalized_text: Subacute infective endocarditis (aortic valve, likely viridans streptococci or enterococci)
Subacute infective endocarditis (aortic.description: Infection of the endocardial surface, often on previously abnormal valves, presenting over weeks to months with low-grade fever, malaise, and new or changing murmurs; aortic valve involvement can produce a diastolic murmur from aortic regurgitation.

Chronic Q fever endocarditis (Coxiella b.description: A chronic infection caused by Coxiella burnetii that preferentially involves damaged or prosthetic valves, presenting with prolonged low-grade fever, malaise, headache, myalgias, and often aortic valve involvement leading to regurgitation and a diastolic murmur.

Brucellosis with endocarditis (aortic va.description: Zoonotic infection that can cause undulant fevers, sweats, malaise, arthralgias, and myalgias; a rare but severe complication is endocarditis, often involving the aortic valve and producing a diastolic murmur.

Ankylosing spondylitis with aortic root.normalized_text: Ankylosing spondylitis with aortic root disease causing aortic regurgitation
Ankylosing spondylitis with aortic root.description: A seronegative spondyloarthropathy that primarily affects the axial skeleton and can involve the aortic root, leading to aortic regurgitation and a diastolic murmur; systemic symptoms can include fatigue and arthralgia.

Libman–Sacks (nonbacterial) endocarditis.normalized_text: Libman–Sacks (nonbacterial) endocarditis associated with systemic lupus erythematosus
Libman–Sacks (nonbacterial) endocarditis.description: Sterile verrucous vegetations on cardiac valves seen in SLE that can produce murmurs; SLE often presents with constitutional symptoms and arthralgia, though prolonged low-grade fever and isolated headache are less typical without other SLE features.

Syphilitic aortitis with aortic regurgit.description: Late (tertiary) syphilis can cause ascending aortitis with dilation of the aortic root, leading to aortic regurgitation and a diastolic murmur; systemic inflammatory symptoms are usually minimal at this late stage.

case: 51-year-old man undergoing venesection for haemochromatosis. During procedure, experienced sudden gurgling sensation up his arm, followed by severe central crushing chest pain with radiation to jaw and left arm, severe dyspnoea, and left sided hemiparesis and dysphasia. On arrival to hospital: hypoxic (oxygen saturation 88% on room air), left hemiplegia (resolved within 15 minutes). Initial ECG showed T-wave inversion inferiorly. Troponin I was raised at 0.14 μg/L (ref 0-0.08 μg/L). Transthoracic echocardiography with bubble study showed right-to-left shunting during normal respiration and Valsalva. Baseline right heart pressures were normal. Transoesophageal echocardiogram confirmed patent foramen ovale with passage of bubbles.

Paradoxical venous air embolism via pate.normalized_text: Paradoxical venous air embolism via patent foramen ovale (PFO) causing coronary and cerebral ischemia
Paradoxical venous air embolism via pate.description: Iatrogenic venous air enters the circulation (e.g., during venesection), traverses a right-to-left shunt (PFO), and embolizes to systemic arteries, causing simultaneous cerebral transient ischemia and coronary ischemia/infarction.

Coronary air embolism (iatrogenic).description: Air introduced into the venous system reaches the coronary arteries (via a right-to-left shunt or retrograde pathway), causing acute myocardial ischemia/infarction.

Venous (pulmonary) air embolism.description: Air enters the venous circulation and lodges in the pulmonary vasculature, causing acute ventilation–perfusion mismatch, hypoxemia, dyspnea, and chest discomfort; can precipitate cardiovascular instability.

Acute coronary syndrome (non–ST-elevatio.description: Myocardial ischemia/infarction due to plaque rupture or supply–demand mismatch, presenting with chest pain, ischemic ECG changes, and elevated cardiac biomarkers.

Aortic dissection.description: An intimal tear in the aorta leads to separation of the aortic wall layers, causing acute severe chest pain and possible neurologic deficits due to branch vessel involvement.

case: 41-year-old right-handed man with neurologic history dating to his early twenties when he presented with seizures. In 2009, he developed headaches. Initial biopsy/resection pathology showed PXA (WHO grade 2) with BRAF V600E mutation confirmed by PCR testing.

Pleomorphic xanthoastrocytoma (PXA), WHO.description: A rare, typically superficial cortical astrocytic tumor that often presents in children and young adults with long-standing seizures; frequently harbors BRAF V600E mutations and can cause headaches.

Anaplastic pleomorphic xanthoastrocytoma.description: A higher-grade variant of PXA characterized by increased mitotic activity and potential for more aggressive behavior; may evolve from grade 2 PXA and can retain BRAF V600E.

Ganglioglioma.description: A mixed neuronal-glial tumor commonly presenting with chronic epilepsy in young patients; a significant subset harbors BRAF V600E mutations.

Dysembryoplastic neuroepithelial tumor (.description: A benign cortical tumor typically presenting in childhood or young adulthood with long-standing drug-resistant focal seizures; headaches are less prominent.

Pilocytic astrocytoma.description: A generally low-grade astrocytoma more common in pediatric/young adult populations; often linked to BRAF pathway alterations (more often KIAA1549-BRAF fusion than V600E); headache is common, seizures less so unless cortical.

case: 32-year-old man with a 10-week history of violaceous rash and progressive muscle weakness. Symptoms began with rash on the eyelids, elbows, metacarpophalangeal and proximal interphalangeal joints, and knees, followed one week later by generalized myalgia and weakness causing difficulty walking, rising from a squat, and climbing stairs. Prior examination showed heliotrope rash, periungual edema, erythematous papules on the fingertips, and moderate-to-severe proximal weakness of the deltoids, triceps, hip flexors, hamstrings, and quadriceps, with normal muscle bulk/tone, reflexes, and sensation. On presentation he was afebrile, tachycardic, hypoxemic on oxygen, with diminished breath sounds at both lung bases, hypoactive bowel sounds, heliotrope rash, erythematous papules on the extensor surfaces of the fingers, elbows, and knees, nontender periungual erythema, pitting edema of the arms and legs, and marked weakness with inability to lift the arms, legs, or head against gravity. Past history included meniscal repair 10 years earlier.

Dermatomyositis (classic).description: An autoimmune idiopathic inflammatory myopathy characterized by pathognomonic cutaneous findings (heliotrope rash, Gottron papules) and symmetric proximal muscle weakness; may be associated with interstitial lung disease and periungual changes.

Antisynthetase syndrome (myositis-associ.description: A subset of idiopathic inflammatory myopathies characterized by anti–tRNA synthetase antibodies and a triad of myositis, interstitial lung disease, and arthritis, often with Raynaud phenomenon and ‘mechanic’s hands’.

Anti-MDA5 dermatomyositis (clinically am.normalized_text: Anti-MDA5 dermatomyositis (clinically amyopathic DM variant with rapidly progressive ILD)
Anti-MDA5 dermatomyositis (clinically am.description: A dermatomyositis subset characterized by violaceous/ulcerative skin lesions, periungual changes, edema, and a high risk of rapidly progressive interstitial lung disease; muscle involvement is often minimal or absent but can occur.

Polymyositis.description: An autoimmune inflammatory myopathy presenting with symmetric proximal muscle weakness without the characteristic dermatologic manifestations of dermatomyositis; may be associated with interstitial lung disease.

Immune-mediated necrotizing myopathy (IM.description: A severe autoimmune myopathy (often anti-SRP or anti-HMGCR mediated) characterized by acute/subacute proximal weakness, very high CK, and muscle fiber necrosis with minimal inflammation; skin rash is uncommon.

case: A 59-year-old woman presented with a longstanding history of epilepsy with complex partial seizures, for which she had been using phenytoin for more than 20 years. She was referred with a 3-year history of progressive muscle weakness, associated with generalized bone and muscle pain, resulting in significant limitations in her daily activities. Her symptoms had further worsened with progressive proximal muscle pain and weakness and increasing bone pain. Physical examination revealed normal renal and liver function. Conventional radiographs demonstrated Looser's zones in the femoral neck bilaterally.

Phenytoin-induced osteomalacia (anticonv.description: Long-term use of enzyme-inducing antiepileptic drugs such as phenytoin accelerates vitamin D catabolism, leading to decreased calcium absorption, secondary hyperparathyroidism, and defective bone mineralization (osteomalacia).

Vitamin D deficiency osteomalacia (non–d.description: Inadequate vitamin D from low intake, limited sunlight exposure, or malabsorption leads to impaired bone mineralization in adults, causing osteomalacia with bone pain, muscle weakness, and pseudofractures.

Anticonvulsant-associated osteoporosis.description: Chronic use of enzyme-inducing antiepileptics can reduce bone mineral density via vitamin D metabolism changes and direct effects on bone turnover, leading to osteoporosis and fracture risk.

Primary hyperparathyroidism (osteitis fi.description: Autonomous parathyroid hormone excess increases bone resorption, causing bone pain, proximal muscle weakness, and skeletal fragility; can present with subperiosteal bone resorption and brown tumors.

Polymyositis.description: An inflammatory myopathy characterized by immune-mediated muscle inflammation leading to progressive proximal muscle weakness and myalgias.

case: A previously healthy 50-year-old man presented with acute-onset dysarthria and was found to be febrile with respiratory distress and lethargy. He performed poorly in the right hand alternating movement test. Physical examination revealed a blood pressure of 130/90 mmHg and heart rate of 116 beats per minute. The apex beat was located in the sixth intercostal space, 1.5 cm outside the midclavicular line. Cardiac auscultation revealed a grade 4/6 systolic murmur that was most prominent at the apex. Laboratory findings showed normal troponin T, creatine kinase (CK), and CK-myoglobin (CK-MB) levels, but elevated N-terminal-pro-brain natriuretic peptide (NT-pro-BNP) levels at 3277 pg/ml. The leukocyte count was 10,620/mm³ with neutrophils at 10,350/mm³, and the erythrocyte sedimentation rate was 68 mm/h. Blood culture was positive for group A β-hemolytic streptococcus. Electrocardiography revealed sinus tachycardia without evidence of ischemia.

Infective endocarditis (mitral valve) du.normalized_text: Infective endocarditis (mitral valve) due to group A Streptococcus
Infective endocarditis (mitral valve) du.description: Infection of the endocardial surface of the heart, often involving heart valves. Left-sided IE can cause new or worsening regurgitant murmurs, systemic sepsis, heart failure, and embolic phenomena.

Acute ischemic stroke due to septic embo.normalized_text: Acute ischemic stroke due to septic emboli
Acute ischemic stroke due to septic embo.description: Acute arterial occlusion of cerebral vessels by embolic material originating from an infected cardiac valve, leading to focal neurologic deficits.

Acute decompensated heart failure due to.normalized_text: Acute decompensated heart failure due to acute severe mitral regurgitation
Acute decompensated heart failure due to.description: Sudden onset of severe mitral regurgitation leads to pulmonary edema and hemodynamic compromise, often presenting with respiratory distress and elevated natriuretic peptides.

Sepsis due to group A Streptococcus with.normalized_text: Sepsis due to group A Streptococcus with sepsis-induced cardiopulmonary dysfunction
Sepsis due to group A Streptococcus with.description: Systemic inflammatory response to infection with organ dysfunction; sepsis can cause tachycardia, respiratory distress, and myocardial depression, elevating natriuretic peptides.

Acute rheumatic carditis (rheumatic feve.normalized_text: Acute rheumatic carditis (rheumatic fever with valvulitis)
Acute rheumatic carditis (rheumatic feve.description: Post-streptococcal autoimmune inflammatory disease that can cause pancarditis and mitral regurgitation, typically occurring weeks after pharyngitis and more common in younger patients.

case: Patient 1: 3.5-year-old male from unrelated Polish parents. Born at 39 weeks gestation with birth weight 3700g (50th-75th centile), length 57cm (97th centile), head circumference 36cm (75th-97th centile), thorax circumference 33cm (25-50th centile), Apgar score 9 at 1 min. Family history unremarkable. Proteinuria, hematuria and glycosuria noted in early neonatal period. UTI at 12 months. At 3 years developed bronchopneumonia with elevated creatinine. Laboratory investigations showed constant proteinuria, glycosuria, hematuria, eGFR (Schwartz) 30.56 ml/min/1.73 m2, elevated serum creatinine, uric acid, urea, total cholesterol, and triglyceride; normal CBC, blood glucose, albumin, thyroid and liver function tests. Renal ultrasound showed increased cortex echogenicity and decreased corticomedullary differentiation. Normal male karyotype (46,XY).

Infantile nephropathic cystinosis (Fanco.normalized_text: Infantile nephropathic cystinosis (Fanconi syndrome due to CTNS)
Infantile nephropathic cystinosis (Fanco.description: An autosomal recessive lysosomal storage disorder causing accumulation of cystine and resulting in generalized proximal renal tubular dysfunction (Fanconi syndrome) that presents in infancy and progresses to chronic kidney disease.

Dent disease (X-linked proximal tubulopa.normalized_text: Dent disease (X-linked proximal tubulopathy due to CLCN5/OCRL variants)
Dent disease (X-linked proximal tubulopa.description: A male-predominant disorder causing low-molecular-weight proteinuria with features of proximal tubule dysfunction and progressive chronic kidney disease; may include hematuria and variably glycosuria.

Oculocerebrorenal syndrome of Lowe (OCRL.normalized_text: Oculocerebrorenal syndrome of Lowe (OCRL-related Fanconi syndrome)
Oculocerebrorenal syndrome of Lowe (OCRL.description: An X-linked disorder characterized by congenital cataracts, neurodevelopmental impairment, and proximal renal tubular dysfunction leading to Fanconi syndrome and chronic kidney disease.

HNF1B-associated nephropathy (RCAD spect.description: A dominantly inherited disorder due to HNF1B variants causing renal developmental abnormalities and tubulointerstitial disease, often with glycosuria and CKD; can be associated with diabetes, hypomagnesemia, and pancreatic/liver anomalies.

Nephronophthisis (juvenile tubulointerst.description: An autosomal recessive tubulointerstitial kidney disease causing progressive CKD in childhood, with kidneys that are echogenic and show loss of corticomedullary differentiation; often associated with polyuria and growth delay.

Alport syndrome (hereditary nephritis).description: A hereditary disorder of type IV collagen causing progressive glomerular disease with hematuria, proteinuria, and eventual CKD, often with sensorineural hearing loss and ocular findings.

Fanconi-Bickel syndrome (GLUT2/SLC2A2 de.description: A rare glycogen storage disease (type XI) characterized by generalized Fanconi syndrome, hepatic glycogen accumulation, and disturbances of glucose homeostasis, often presenting in infancy.

case: A 58-year-old man presented with a six-week history of muscle weakness, dysphagia, and a symmetrical widespread rash on the face, torso, and limbs. Laboratory testing revealed elevated creatine kinase of 7070 u/L (reference range 30-175). An oesophagogastroduodenoscopy was performed and showed abnormal findings, and a PET CT scan was arranged.

Dermatomyositis (possible malignancy-ass.description: An autoimmune inflammatory myopathy characterized by proximal muscle weakness and distinctive cutaneous eruptions; in older adults it is often associated with underlying malignancy and can involve the oropharyngeal/esophageal muscles causing dysphagia.

Immune-mediated necrotizing myopathy (e..normalized_text: Immune-mediated necrotizing myopathy (e.g., anti-HMGCR or anti-SRP, often statin-associated)
Immune-mediated necrotizing myopathy (e..description: A severe autoimmune myopathy characterized by acute or subacute proximal muscle weakness, very high CK, and myonecrosis with minimal inflammation; can be triggered by statins or occur idiopathically; dysphagia may occur.

Polymyositis.description: An idiopathic inflammatory myopathy causing symmetric proximal muscle weakness and elevated muscle enzymes; can involve the pharyngeal/esophageal musculature leading to dysphagia; lacks the pathognomonic rash of dermatomyositis.

Inclusion body myositis.description: A chronic, progressive myopathy typically in older adults, often with asymmetric weakness of finger flexors and quadriceps, frequent dysphagia, and modest CK elevations; rash is not a feature.

Myasthenia gravis.description: An autoimmune neuromuscular junction disorder causing fluctuating skeletal muscle weakness, commonly affecting bulbar muscles leading to dysphagia; muscle enzymes are typically normal and no rash is expected.

case: An 8-year-old boy presented to his general practitioner with limping and complaints of occasional leg pain. He was otherwise healthy and afebrile. On physical examination, he walked with a limp and demonstrated painful, reduced internal rotation and abduction of his right hip. Plain radiographs were obtained to evaluate his symptoms.

Legg-Calvé-Perthes disease.description: Idiopathic avascular necrosis of the femoral head in children, typically ages 4–8, presenting with insidious limp, hip/knee pain, and limited hip abduction and internal rotation.

Transient synovitis of the hip.description: Self-limited inflammatory condition of the hip joint in young children, often following a viral illness, characterized by acute onset limp and limited painful hip motion with little or no fever.

Slipped capital femoral epiphysis (SCFE).description: Displacement of the femoral head relative to the neck through the growth plate, typically in early adolescence, causing hip or knee pain, limp, and decreased hip internal rotation.

Septic arthritis of the hip.description: Acute bacterial infection of the hip joint that causes severe pain, limited range of motion, and systemic illness; an orthopedic emergency.

Osteoid osteoma (proximal femur/hip regi.description: A benign bone tumor common in children and adolescents, causing focal pain classically worse at night and relieved by NSAIDs; can cause limp if near the hip.

case: A 62-year-old fit and well Romanian man presented with a two-week history of worsening acute localized pain in the upper abdomen and vomiting. His surgical history included an open appendectomy as a child and laparoscopic cholecystectomy 20 years ago. On presentation, he had fever (39°C) and tachycardia (104 beats/min), with blood pressure of 125/73 mm Hg. Physical examination revealed generalized abdominal tenderness, worse in the right upper quadrant, with localized guarding in the right upper quadrant. Blood tests showed a raised white cell count of 16 × 10⁹/L (reference range 4-10 × 10⁹/L) and a C reactive protein concentration of 277 mg/L (reference value <9 mg/L). A frontal projection erect chest radiograph was initially reported as showing pneumoperitoneum, but showed a normal bowel gas pattern under the left hemidiaphragm.

Acute ascending cholangitis.description: Bacterial infection of the biliary tree due to obstruction (often from choledocholithiasis or strictures), leading to sepsis.

Pyogenic liver abscess.description: A collection of pus within the liver, often arising from biliary infections, portal venous spread, or hematogenous seeding.

Right-sided colonic diverticulitis.description: Inflammation or infection of diverticula in the right colon (cecum/hepatic flexure), which can present with RUQ pain and systemic inflammatory response.

Acute pancreatitis.description: Acute inflammation of the pancreas, commonly due to gallstones or alcohol, presenting with acute upper abdominal pain and systemic inflammation.

Chilaiditi syndrome (symptomatic colonic.description: Interposition of colon between the liver and right hemidiaphragm causing symptoms and mimicking pneumoperitoneum on radiographs.

case: A 1-year and 4-month-old girl was admitted for evaluation of psychomotor retardation and an operation for exotropia. She was born at term (gestational age: 40 weeks) by cesarean delivery after an uneventful pregnancy, and was the first child of healthy, unrelated parents. The family history was unremarkable. On admission, she presented with a characteristic high-pitched cry and microcephaly. She showed delayed motor functions and crawling, was able to sit unassisted but unable to stand, with developmental characteristics lagging behind for normal chronologic age. On neurologic examination, she had left leg hypotonia, with normal tendon reflexes and normal cranial nerve signs. When she was 6 months old, ventricular septal defect was detected by echocardiography. Chromosome analysis revealed 46,XX,del (5) (p15.2) one month after delivery.

Cri-du-chat syndrome (5p deletion syndro.description: A congenital disorder caused by deletion of the short arm of chromosome 5 (typically 5p15), characterized by a distinctive high-pitched cat-like cry in infancy, microcephaly, global developmental delay, hypotonia, dysmorphic features, and frequent congenital heart defects and strabismus.

Rett syndrome.description: A neurodevelopmental disorder predominantly in girls due to MECP2 mutations, characterized by normal early development followed by regression between 6–18 months, acquired microcephaly, loss of purposeful hand skills with stereotypies, gait abnormalities, and severe language impairment.

Angelman syndrome.description: A neurogenetic disorder typically due to loss of maternal UBE3A expression, marked by severe developmental delay, microcephaly, ataxia, seizures, minimal speech, and a characteristic happy demeanor with frequent laughter.

Wolf-Hirschhorn syndrome (4p deletion).description: A contiguous gene deletion syndrome due to loss on chromosome 4p, presenting with severe growth restriction, microcephaly, distinctive 'Greek helmet' facial features, hypotonia, seizures, intellectual disability, and frequent congenital heart defects.

22q11.2 deletion syndrome (DiGeorge/velo.description: A microdeletion syndrome characterized by conotruncal cardiac defects, palatal abnormalities, immune deficiency, hypocalcemia, learning and developmental delays, and characteristic facial features.

case: A 7-year-old girl with no past medical history had intermittent abdominal pain for about 1 month, unrelieved by anti-inflammatory treatment. Abdominal CT showed peritoneal effusion and retroperitoneal lymphadenopathy. Serum AFP was elevated to 1,210 ng/mL. Ultrasound showed multiple enlarged abdominal and retroperitoneal hypoechoic lymph nodes. The ovaries, fallopian tubes, uterus, cervix, and vagina were unremarkable. At surgery, a 4 cm jejunal mass involving the full thickness of the jejunum was found.

diagnoses.normalized_text: Primary yolk sac tumor of intestine

Extragonadal yolk sac tumor (endodermal.normalized_text: Extragonadal yolk sac tumor (endodermal sinus tumor) of the small intestine
Extragonadal yolk sac tumor (endodermal.description: A malignant germ cell tumor arising outside the gonads that secretes alpha-fetoprotein (AFP). Rarely, it can originate in the gastrointestinal tract, including the small intestine, and metastasize to regional nodes.

Burkitt lymphoma (intestinal involvement.description: An aggressive B-cell non-Hodgkin lymphoma common in children that frequently involves the ileocecal or small bowel region, presenting with abdominal mass, pain, and lymphadenopathy.

Gastrointestinal stromal tumor (pediatri.normalized_text: Gastrointestinal stromal tumor (pediatric GIST) of the small intestine
Gastrointestinal stromal tumor (pediatri.description: A mesenchymal tumor of the GI tract driven by KIT/PDGFRA or SDH alterations; pediatric cases often differ biologically from adult GIST and can occur in the small bowel.

Inflammatory myofibroblastic tumor (IMT).normalized_text: Inflammatory myofibroblastic tumor (IMT) of the small intestine
Inflammatory myofibroblastic tumor (IMT).description: A rare pediatric tumor composed of myofibroblasts and inflammatory cells that can involve the mesentery or bowel, presenting with abdominal pain and a mass.

Hepatoid adenocarcinoma of the small int.normalized_text: Hepatoid adenocarcinoma of the small intestine (AFP-producing GI carcinoma)
Hepatoid adenocarcinoma of the small int.description: A rare adenocarcinoma with hepatocellular differentiation that produces AFP; primary sites include the stomach and, rarely, small intestine, often with nodal metastases and ascites.

Hepatoblastoma with peritoneal/intestina.description: The most common primary liver cancer in young children that produces AFP; advanced cases can seed the peritoneum, causing ascites and abdominal masses.

case: 6-month-old boy with 2 days of intermittent nocturnal abdominal pain causing crying and drawing up of the legs, with episodes of abdominal rigidity. He developed three bowel movements with progressively increasing red blood, the last nearly all blood with a large clot. History includes infantile colic and gastroesophageal reflux treated with ranitidine; recently started pureed foods and was on low-lactose cow milk-based formula. On exam he had diffuse abdominal tenderness, worse on the right, no masses or anal fissures, and later became pale with tachycardia and lower blood pressure.

Ileocolic intussusception.description: Telescoping of a segment of intestine into an adjacent segment, most commonly ileum into colon in infants, causing venous congestion, ischemia, colicky pain, and sometimes mucosal sloughing with bleeding.

Meckel diverticulum with bleeding (± as.normalized_text: Meckel diverticulum with bleeding (± as a lead point for intussusception)
Meckel diverticulum with bleeding (± as.description: Congenital true diverticulum of the distal ileum that may contain ectopic gastric mucosa, leading to painless lower GI bleeding; can also act as a lead point for intussusception, adding colicky pain.

Midgut volvulus due to malrotation.description: Torsion of the intestine around a narrow mesenteric base in malrotation, leading to bowel ischemia, severe pain, and potentially hematochezia and shock.

Allergic proctocolitis (cow’s milk prote.normalized_text: Allergic proctocolitis (cow’s milk protein induced colitis)
Allergic proctocolitis (cow’s milk prote.description: Inflammatory reaction of the distal colon in infants to dietary proteins (often cow’s milk/soy), causing blood-streaked stools in otherwise well infants.

Infectious colitis (e.g., Shigella, Salm.description: Bacterial infection of the colon causing inflammatory diarrhea with abdominal pain and hematochezia.

Henoch–Schönlein purpura (IgA vasculitis.normalized_text: Henoch–Schönlein purpura (IgA vasculitis) with gastrointestinal involvement
Henoch–Schönlein purpura (IgA vasculitis.description: Small-vessel IgA-mediated vasculitis in children that can cause colicky abdominal pain, GI bleeding, and potential intussusception in addition to purpuric rash and arthralgias.

case: A 69-year-old female non-smoker presented with a 6-month history of progressive breathlessness. She had no relevant past medical history or drug history. Spirometry showed FEV1 32% predicted and a flow-volume loop suggesting severe small airway disease. Transthoracic echocardiogram was normal.

diagnoses.normalized_text: Diffuse idiopathic pulmonary neuroendocrine cell hyperplasia
diagnoses.icd11_title: Diffuse idiopathic pulmonary neuroendocrine cell hyperplasia

Constrictive (obliterative) bronchioliti.description: A small-airways disease characterized by inflammation and fibrosis leading to luminal narrowing and airflow obstruction; often presents with progressive dyspnea and obstructive spirometry with minimal reversibility.

Late-onset asthma.description: Chronic inflammatory airway disease causing variable airflow limitation and bronchial hyperresponsiveness; can present de novo in older adults.

Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (C.normalized_text: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) in a non-smoker
Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (C.description: Persistent airflow limitation due to airway/alveolar abnormalities; typically from smoking but can result from biomass exposure, occupational exposures, or prior severe infections.

Hypersensitivity pneumonitis (airway-pre.description: Immune-mediated lung disease due to inhaled antigens causing small-airway inflammation; can present with dyspnea and mixed or obstructive physiology, especially in chronic forms.

Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency–related e.description: Genetic deficiency leading to panacinar emphysema and airflow obstruction, often in non-smokers or with minimal smoking; classically lower-lobe predominant.

Diffuse panbronchiolitis.description: Chronic inflammatory small-airways disease characterized by diffuse involvement of respiratory bronchioles; classically seen in East Asian populations with chronic sinusitis and obstructive physiology.

case: 27-year-old man with a few days of cough, hemoptysis, and low-grade fever. He denied night sweats and weight loss. History notable for left supraclavicular lymph node enlargement that had fluctuated since age 15. On examination, he was thin, with low-grade fever, mild hypoxemia, left upper lung crackles, and a 2 cm left supraclavicular lymph node that was nontender, firm, nonfixed, circumscribed, and rubbery. Labs showed leukocytosis with neutrophilia, elevated ESR and CRP, and elevated soluble IL-2 receptor. Blood and sputum cultures were negative, as were serologies for ANCA, rheumatoid factor, HIV, and tumor markers. Otologic evaluation was unremarkable. Transbronchial lung biopsy showed granulomatous inflammation without identified pathogens.

Sarcoidosis.description: A multisystem granulomatous disease characterized by noncaseating granulomas, most commonly affecting the lungs and intrathoracic lymph nodes, and often associated with elevated soluble IL-2 receptor.

Pulmonary tuberculosis (TB).description: Mycobacterial infection that commonly involves the lungs, causing caseating granulomas; classic symptoms include chronic cough, weight loss, night sweats, fever, and hemoptysis.

Granulomatosis with polyangiitis (GPA).description: A necrotizing granulomatous vasculitis affecting small to medium vessels, commonly involving the upper and lower respiratory tracts and kidneys; hemoptysis can occur with pulmonary involvement.

Hypersensitivity pneumonitis.description: Immune-mediated interstitial lung disease due to inhaled antigens, characterized by poorly formed noncaseating granulomas, cough, dyspnea, and hypoxemia.

Hodgkin lymphoma with pulmonary involvem.normalized_text: Hodgkin lymphoma with pulmonary involvement or sarcoid-like reaction
Hodgkin lymphoma with pulmonary involvem.description: A lymphoid malignancy characterized by Reed-Sternberg cells and classically presenting with painless, rubbery lymphadenopathy; can occasionally involve the lungs or provoke sarcoid-like granulomatous reactions.

Pulmonary histoplasmosis (or other endem.normalized_text: Pulmonary histoplasmosis (or other endemic fungal granulomatous infection)
Pulmonary histoplasmosis (or other endem.description: Infection by Histoplasma capsulatum (or similar fungi), causing pulmonary granulomas and mediastinal lymphadenopathy; presentations range from asymptomatic to subacute pulmonary disease with cough and fever.

case: A 31-year-old Caucasian man with multiple sclerosis who had received 24 natalizumab infusions and was switched to fingolimod due to persistent high anti-JCPyV antibody index (3.61). After 40 days of fingolimod treatment, he developed seizures and visual field defects. Neurological examination revealed lateral nystagmus to the left, homonymous hemianopia, distal tremor and spasm of the upper limbs. He presented with leukopenia (0.83 × 10^9/L) at hospital admission.

Progressive multifocal leukoencephalopat.normalized_text: Progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (PML) due to JC virus
Progressive multifocal leukoencephalopat.description: Opportunistic demyelinating disease caused by JC virus reactivation in the setting of immunosuppression, strongly associated with natalizumab exposure and high anti-JC virus antibody index.

PML-associated immune reconstitution inf.description: Paradoxical inflammatory worsening of PML lesions due to immune reconstitution after withdrawal of natalizumab; can occur within weeks to months after stopping natalizumab, sometimes even when switched to another agent.

Posterior reversible encephalopathy synd.description: Reversible vasogenic edema of the posterior circulation often triggered by cytotoxic/immunosuppressive drugs, hypertension, or renal failure; presents with seizures and visual disturbances.

Multiple sclerosis relapse with occipita.normalized_text: Multiple sclerosis relapse with occipital/cortical involvement
Multiple sclerosis relapse with occipita.description: An acute demyelinating relapse affecting visual pathways and cortical regions in a patient with MS, potentially leading to visual field deficits and, less commonly, seizures.

Cerebral venous sinus thrombosis (CVST).normalized_text: Cerebral venous sinus thrombosis (CVST) with occipital involvement
Cerebral venous sinus thrombosis (CVST).description: Thrombosis of cerebral venous sinuses leading to venous congestion, infarction, and seizures; can cause visual field defects if occipital lobes are involved.

case: A 39-year-old Korean male presented with intermittent and atypical chest discomfort symptoms. His medical history included burning pain originating in the extremities and radiating inwards to the limbs since childhood, which was previously dismissed as 'growing pains'. He also experienced ringing in the ears, had angiokeratomas on his trunk, and cornea verticillata. Physical examination revealed proteinuria (P/C ratio 0.501) without hematuria and normal renal function. His plasma αGal-A activity was markedly lower than controls at 4.1 nmoL/hr/mg protein (normal cutoff >35 nmoL/hr/mg protein). Genetic testing identified a hemizygous mutation in exon 4 of GLA, c.617T>C (p.Leu206 Pro).

Fabry disease (Anderson-Fabry disease).description: An X-linked lysosomal storage disorder caused by deficient alpha-galactosidase A (GLA) activity leading to globotriaosylceramide (Gb3) accumulation, with neuropathic pain, angiokeratomas, cornea verticillata, renal and cardiac involvement, and auditory/vestibular symptoms.

Alport syndrome.description: A hereditary nephropathy due to mutations in type IV collagen (COL4A3/A4/A5) characterized by progressive renal disease with hematuria, sensorineural hearing loss, and ocular abnormalities (e.g., anterior lenticonus, dot-and-fleck retinopathy).

Fucosidosis (alpha-L-fucosidase deficien.description: A rare autosomal recessive lysosomal storage disorder caused by deficiency of alpha-L-fucosidase, leading to accumulation of fucose-containing glycoproteins and glycolipids; features can include developmental delay, coarse facies, angiokeratomas, recurrent infections, and neurologic involvement.

Schindler disease type 2 (Kanzaki diseas.normalized_text: Schindler disease type 2 (Kanzaki disease; alpha-N-acetylgalactosaminidase deficiency)
Schindler disease type 2 (Kanzaki diseas.description: A rare lysosomal storage disorder characterized by deficiency of alpha-N-acetylgalactosaminidase leading to angiokeratomas, peripheral neuropathy, and sometimes hearing loss; typically adult-onset with dermatologic findings.

Idiopathic small fiber neuropathy.description: A peripheral neuropathy affecting small unmyelinated fibers, causing burning pain, dysesthesias, and autonomic symptoms; etiologies include diabetes, autoimmune, toxins, or idiopathic.

case: A multitrauma patient was admitted to the intensive care unit (ICU) due to an intrahepatic hematoma. On the 7th day of ICU hospitalization, he presented fever. Laboratory blood tests showed leucocytosis and elevated liver function values.

Infected intrahepatic hematoma (hepatic.description: Bacterial superinfection of a pre-existing intrahepatic hematoma leading to a hepatic abscess, common in trauma patients and presents with systemic signs of infection and liver test abnormalities.

Acalculous cholecystitis.description: Inflammation and infection of the gallbladder without stones, occurring in critically ill ICU patients and associated with sepsis and cholestatic liver enzyme elevations.

Acute cholangitis.description: Bacterial infection of the biliary tree typically due to obstruction, presenting with fever, leukocytosis, and cholestatic liver enzyme elevation; can occur nosocomially.

Catheter-related bloodstream infection (.description: Nosocomial bacteremia originating from an intravascular catheter; can cause fever and leukocytosis and may lead to sepsis-associated cholestasis with elevated liver enzymes.

Ventilator-associated pneumonia (VAP) or.description: Nosocomial pneumonia developing after 48 hours of hospitalization or ventilation, presenting with fever and leukocytosis; may cause secondary sepsis with mild liver enzyme elevations.

Drug-induced liver injury (DILI).description: Liver injury caused by medications (e.g., antibiotics, antiepileptics, parenteral nutrition) commonly used in ICU; may present with fever, leukocytosis (if hypersensitivity), and elevated liver enzymes.

Ischemic hepatitis (shock liver).description: Hepatocellular injury due to hepatic hypoperfusion, often in the setting of shock or severe hypotension; characterized by markedly elevated transaminases more than cholestatic enzymes; fever is not a core feature.

case: A 57-year-old man presented to the emergency department with a 12-hour history of hematuria. Several hours after intravenous urography was performed with iodinated contrast material, generalized pustular eruptions developed, with multiple coalescing vesicles and pus-filled bullae observed on the trunk, arms, and legs. Laboratory studies revealed neutrophilia and mild eosinophilia with 55% neutrophils and 8% eosinophils, and a white-cell count of 6500 per cubic millimeter. Histopathological examination of the lesions showed pseudoepitheliomatous hyperplasia, full-thickness epidermal necrosis, and a diffuse neutrophilic dermal infiltrate. Microbiologic studies were negative.

Acute generalized exanthematous pustulos.description: A severe, acute pustular drug reaction characterized by sudden onset of numerous sterile, non-follicular pustules on an erythematous base, often within hours to a few days after exposure to a culprit medication (including iodinated contrast), accompanied by neutrophilia and sometimes eosinophilia; typically resolves after withdrawal of the trigger.

Stevens–Johnson syndrome/toxic epidermal.description: A severe mucocutaneous drug reaction characterized by extensive keratinocyte apoptosis leading to full-thickness epidermal necrosis and detachment; usually occurs 1–3 weeks after drug initiation and often involves mucous membranes; may be triggered by various drugs including contrast media.

Generalized pustular psoriasis (von Zumb.description: An acute, potentially life-threatening form of psoriasis characterized by widespread pustules on erythematous skin, systemic inflammation, and neutrophilia; may be triggered by drugs, infections, or withdrawal of systemic corticosteroids.

Sweet syndrome (acute febrile neutrophil.normalized_text: Sweet syndrome (acute febrile neutrophilic dermatosis), drug-induced
Sweet syndrome (acute febrile neutrophil.description: An acute neutrophilic dermatosis presenting with tender, erythematous plaques and a dense neutrophilic infiltrate in the dermis, often associated with fever and leukocytosis; can be triggered by medications and less commonly presents with vesiculopustular or bullous lesions.

case: 54-year-old female with hypertension and hyperlipidemia presented to cardiology clinic for follow-up 20 months since her most recent office visit. She was being evaluated for follow-up of cardiac risk factors and medication management. The patient was in her usual state of health and asymptomatic without changes in her exercise tolerance, weight, or energy levels. She did not have any gross hematuria or flank pain.

45-year-old man with acute illness after dog bites. He developed nausea, epigastric pain, and vomiting the day before admission. Three days earlier, he had been bitten on the hands and forearms while bathing his dog; he also had head trauma from a rusty nail a few days earlier and dental extractions 1–2 weeks earlier. Past history included asthma, mild COPD, anxiety, depression, chronic back pain, and alcohol abuse with heavy recent intake. On exam, he was ill-appearing, anxious, and diaphoretic with hypothermia, tachycardia, tachypnea, and elevated blood pressure. He had multiple lacerations with necrotic edges and scratch marks on the hands and forearms, including a 3–4 cm right forearm lesion with a 5–7 cm surrounding purplish border, and capillary refill of 5 seconds.

Capnocytophaga canimorsus sepsis.description: A severe, rapidly progressive sepsis caused by Capnocytophaga species commonly found in the oral flora of dogs; high risk in people with alcohol use disorder, cirrhosis, or asplenia after dog bites or scratches.

Necrotizing soft tissue infection (necro.description: A rapidly progressive, life-threatening infection of fascia and subcutaneous tissues often caused by polymicrobial flora or group A Streptococcus, sometimes following traumatic wounds or animal bites.

Pasteurella multocida cellulitis with po.normalized_text: Pasteurella multocida cellulitis with possible bacteremia
Pasteurella multocida cellulitis with po.description: A common rapidly developing soft tissue infection following dog or cat bites caused by Pasteurella species; can progress to systemic illness, especially in high-risk hosts.

Clostridial myonecrosis (gas gangrene).description: A fulminant soft tissue infection due to Clostridium species causing muscle necrosis, systemic toxicity, and potentially crepitus; can follow traumatic wounds contaminated with soil or devitalized tissue.

Tetanus.description: A neurotoxic illness caused by Clostridium tetani following contaminated wounds; presents with trismus, muscle rigidity, and spasms after an incubation period of days to weeks.

case: 27-year-old female, 162cm tall, 30kg weight. Born after normal pregnancy/delivery. No family history of neurological diseases. Normal early development. At age 6, developed general muscle weakness and gait disturbance with decreased muscle tone/strength and atrophic muscle mass. At age 8, muscle biopsy showed mitochondrial myopathy of pleoconial type. At age 24, had sudden syncope. At age 26, had stroke with general weakness, aphagia, and dysarthria. Current presentation at age 27 with left hemiplegia and aphasia. Lab findings: plasma lactate 21.8 mg/dL (elevated), normal CBC/electrolytes/BUN/creatinine, free T4 1.76 ng/dL, TSH 0.04 μIU/mL, C3 13 mg/dL (low), C4 18 mg/dL (normal). Negative for ASO antibody, rheumatoid factor, anti-dsDNA, lupus anticoagulants, and anti-cytoplasmic antibody. DNA sequencing showed m.3303C>T mutation in mitochondrial tRNA leucine 1 gene.

diagnoses.name: MELAS syndrome
diagnoses.icd11_title: MELAS - [Mitochondrial encephalopathy with lactic acidosis and stroke-like episodes] syndrome

MELAS (Mitochondrial Encephalomyopathy,.normalized_text: MELAS (Mitochondrial Encephalomyopathy, Lactic Acidosis, and Stroke-like episodes)
MELAS (Mitochondrial Encephalomyopathy,.description: A mitochondrial disorder, often due to MT-TL1 (tRNA-Leu(UUR)) mutations, characterized by childhood-onset myopathy, lactic acidosis, and recurrent stroke-like episodes causing focal neurological deficits.

MERRF (Myoclonic Epilepsy with Ragged Re.normalized_text: MERRF (Myoclonic Epilepsy with Ragged Red Fibers)
MERRF (Myoclonic Epilepsy with Ragged Re.description: A mitochondrial disorder classically presenting with myoclonus, epilepsy, ataxia, and ragged red fibers on biopsy; due to various mtDNA mutations, often tRNA genes.

Leigh syndrome (subacute necrotizing enc.description: A mitochondrial disorder typically presenting in infancy or early childhood with progressive neurodegeneration, lactic acidosis, and brainstem/basal ganglia lesions.

Hyperthyroidism/Thyrotoxicosis.description: Excess thyroid hormone state causing weight loss, heat intolerance, tremor, tachycardia, and proximal muscle weakness; can exacerbate catabolic state and weakness.

Antiphospholipid syndrome (APS).description: An autoimmune prothrombotic condition causing arterial and venous thrombosis and pregnancy morbidity; can lead to ischemic stroke in young patients.

case: 29-year-old woman with a 7-week history of progressive generalized pruritus, nausea, bloating, and watery mustard-colored diarrhea დაწყ after eating sushi. Three weeks later, she developed jaundice, right upper quadrant discomfort, decreased appetite, and amber-colored urine. Initial urgent care treatment with methylprednisolone, hydroxyzine, and diphenoxylate-atropine did not help. Prior labs showed elevated ALT 327 U/L, AST 104 U/L, total bilirubin 5.8 mg/dL, and CA 19-9 73 U/mL. Past history included anxiety and depression; she took no medications and had no drug allergies. On exam, she was thin, jaundiced with scleral icterus, and had diffuse excoriations. Vital signs were stable.

Acute hepatitis A.description: A self-limited viral hepatitis transmitted fecal-orally, often via contaminated food (including raw/undercooked shellfish or food-handled items), causing acute hepatocellular injury and cholestasis.

Acute hepatitis E.description: An acute viral hepatitis transmitted enterically; more severe in pregnancy but can affect others, leading to jaundice and cholestatic features.

Liver fluke infection (Clonorchis/Opisth.description: Parasitic trematode infection acquired by ingesting raw/undercooked freshwater fish, causing biliary inflammation, cholestasis, and pruritus; can mildly raise CA 19-9.

Choledocholithiasis (common bile duct st.normalized_text: Choledocholithiasis (common bile duct stone) causing obstructive jaundice
Choledocholithiasis (common bile duct st.description: A gallstone obstructing the common bile duct, leading to conjugated hyperbilirubinemia, pruritus, dark urine, and cholestatic liver injury; CA 19-9 can be elevated in benign obstruction.

Autoimmune hepatitis.description: Immune-mediated hepatocellular inflammation, often in young women, presenting with elevated transaminases, jaundice, and sometimes pruritus.

Primary biliary cholangitis.description: Chronic autoimmune destruction of small intrahepatic bile ducts leading to cholestasis, pruritus, and later jaundice; most common in middle-aged women.

case: A patient with known Crohn's disease presented with difficulties to pass stool, a sensation of a foreign body in the rectum and limited rectal bleeding. An endoscopy was performed as the first examination. A gallstone was found in the rectum and it was removed without complications.

Rectal gallstone impaction (gallstone co.description: A large gallstone migrates through a cholecystoenteric fistula and becomes lodged in the distal colon or rectum, causing obstructive symptoms, tenesmus, and minor mucosal trauma.

Gallstone ileus due to cholecystoenteric.normalized_text: Gallstone ileus due to cholecystoenteric fistula
Gallstone ileus due to cholecystoenteric.description: A fistula between the gallbladder and gastrointestinal tract allows a gallstone to enter the bowel lumen, potentially causing distal obstruction; stones may rarely traverse to and lodge in the rectum.

Crohn's disease–related anorectal strict.description: Chronic inflammation and fibrosis from Crohn's disease can cause anorectal strictures, leading to obstructed defecation, tenesmus-like sensations, and occasional minor bleeding.

Hemorrhoids (especially prolapsed intern.description: Dilated hemorrhoidal veins can cause painless, limited rectal bleeding; prolapse can produce a sensation of rectal fullness or a foreign body.

Fecal impaction.description: Hardened stool mass in the rectum causes outlet obstruction, fullness/foreign body sensation, and may lead to minor mucosal trauma with limited bleeding.

case: 15-year-old boy presented after injuring his left knee while carrying a tray of food at a fast food restaurant. He felt his knee 'wobble' and fell to the floor, unable to bear weight due to pain. Medical history included chronic fatigue syndrome. Had a Beighton score of 6 (indicating joint laxity) but no history of joint dislocations. On examination: laterally dislocated patella, moderate effusion, pain on palpation around medial patellofemoral ligament, range of movement reduced to extension-flexion of 0/10/60 degrees, ligamentous tests unremarkable. Two weeks later: complained of intermittent locking in left knee, had joint effusion and palpable loose body under patella.

Acute lateral patellar dislocation with.normalized_text: Acute lateral patellar dislocation with osteochondral fracture/loose body
Acute lateral patellar dislocation with.description: First-time traumatic lateral displacement of the patella, commonly tearing the medial patellofemoral ligament and causing osteochondral injury that can create a loose body and mechanical locking.

Medial patellofemoral ligament (MPFL) te.description: Disruption of the MPFL, the primary soft-tissue restraint to lateral patellar translation, typically occurring with a lateral patellar dislocation and causing medial knee pain and instability.

Patellofemoral instability due to genera.normalized_text: Patellofemoral instability due to generalized joint hypermobility
Patellofemoral instability due to genera.description: Patellar subluxation/dislocation precipitated by ligamentous laxity (hypermobility spectrum), common in adolescents and predisposes to instability with relatively minor trauma.

Osteochondritis dissecans (OCD) of the k.normalized_text: Osteochondritis dissecans (OCD) of the knee with loose body
Osteochondritis dissecans (OCD) of the k.description: Subchondral bone lesion in adolescents that can lead to instability of the overlying cartilage, generating intra-articular loose bodies and causing effusions and mechanical locking.

Bucket-handle meniscal tear.description: A displaced longitudinal meniscal tear that can cause true mechanical locking, effusion, and pain, often after a twisting injury.

case: 45-year-old female with 13-year history of papular spiny eruptions on trunk and limbs with severe pruritus. Patient was otherwise in good health. Family history positive for psoriasis in sister. Treatment history included topical steroids and oral antihistamines without relief. Papular lesions on body presented before the alopecia of scalp and pubis, while axillae had been involved for 6 years.

Graham-Little–Piccardi–Lassueur syndrome.description: A rare variant of lichen planopilaris characterized by a triad of scarring alopecia of the scalp, non-scarring alopecia of the axillae/pubic areas, and widespread follicular keratotic (spiny) papules on the trunk and limbs; often pruritic and more common in middle-aged women.

Lichen planopilaris (follicular lichen p.description: An inflammatory lymphocytic cicatricial alopecia (lichen planus of hair follicles) that can present with scarring scalp alopecia and follicular keratotic papules over the trunk and extremities; often pruritic.

Pityriasis rubra pilaris (PRP).description: A chronic papulosquamous disorder with follicular hyperkeratosis, erythematous plaques (often orange-hued), ‘islands of sparing,’ and possible scalp involvement; can be pruritic and chronic.

Follicular (spiny) psoriasis.description: A rare variant of psoriasis featuring numerous small, spiny, hyperkeratotic follicular papules; may coexist with typical psoriatic plaques. Family history may be present.

Lichen spinulosus.description: A benign follicular keratotic disorder characterized by grouped patches of spiny papules, often in adolescents or young adults; lesions can be pruritic but usually lack associated alopecia.

case: 35-year-old woman with severe hypertension, edema, and renal failure. She had preeclampsia in a pregnancy 12 months earlier, requiring Caesarean delivery at 29 weeks, followed by persistent poorly controlled hypertension and proteinuria >1 g/day. Six months before admission, she developed fatigue, headaches, worsening hypertension, and facial/pedal edema. On presentation she was pale with blood pressure 151/103 mmHg. Labs showed severe anemia, thrombocytopenia, marked renal dysfunction, increased reticulocytes, schistocytes, heavy proteinuria (4.9 g/24 h), hematuria, elevated LDH and bilirubin, low haptoglobin, and a negative Coombs test. Liver enzymes were normal, and immunologic, viral, and antiphospholipid antibody tests were negative.

Atypical hemolytic uremic syndrome (comp.normalized_text: Atypical hemolytic uremic syndrome (complement-mediated TMA, postpartum aHUS)
Atypical hemolytic uremic syndrome (comp.description: A complement dysregulation–mediated thrombotic microangiopathy often triggered by pregnancy/postpartum, characterized by microangiopathic hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia, severe renal failure, and hypertension.

Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP.description: An ADAMTS13 deficiency–related thrombotic microangiopathy causing microangiopathic hemolytic anemia and thrombocytopenia, often with neurologic symptoms; renal involvement is variable.

Malignant hypertension–associated thromb.description: Severe, sustained hypertension can cause endothelial injury leading to a thrombotic microangiopathy with microangiopathic hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia, acute kidney injury, and proteinuria/hematuria.

Preeclampsia/HELLP-related thrombotic mi.description: Preeclampsia and HELLP syndrome are pregnancy-related disorders that can cause TMA with hemolysis, thrombocytopenia, and renal dysfunction; typically occur in late pregnancy or early postpartum.

Membranous nephropathy (primary or secon.description: A glomerular disease characterized by immune complex deposition causing heavy proteinuria, edema, and hypertension; can lead to chronic kidney disease.

case: 45-year-old woman presented with syncope and severe anemia (hemoglobin 6 g/dL) with lower GI bleeding. A diagnostic colonoscopy was negative. CT scan of abdomen and pelvis revealed a 3.2 x 3 x 2.9 cm contrast-enhancing right lower-quadrant mass arising from the wall of the ileum. No evidence of metastatic disease. Subsequent laparotomy found a 3.5 cm mass that was resected with negative margins. Molecular studies showed a 42-base pair deletion in exon 11 of the KIT gene (V559_D572del) that would delete all or part of codons 558 to 572 and would change the 558-encoding amino acid from Lys to Asn (K558N).

diagnoses.name: Gastrointestinal stromal tumor
diagnoses.icd11_title: Gastrointestinal stromal tumour of unspecified gastrointestinal sites

Gastrointestinal stromal tumor (GIST) of.normalized_text: Gastrointestinal stromal tumor (GIST) of the ileum
Gastrointestinal stromal tumor (GIST) of.description: A mesenchymal tumor of the gastrointestinal tract arising from interstitial cells of Cajal, commonly driven by activating KIT mutations; small-bowel GISTs often present with occult or overt GI bleeding and anemia.

Small bowel adenocarcinoma (ileal).description: A malignant epithelial tumor of the small intestine that can present with bleeding, anemia, obstruction, or abdominal pain; often diagnosed late due to nonspecific symptoms.

Ileal neuroendocrine tumor (carcinoid tu.description: A well-differentiated neuroendocrine neoplasm commonly arising in the distal small bowel; may present with bleeding, obstruction, or carcinoid syndrome when metastatic.

Primary small bowel lymphoma.description: A lymphoid malignancy involving the small intestine (e.g., diffuse large B-cell lymphoma, MALT, or enteropathy-associated T-cell lymphoma), presenting with mass, bleeding, weight loss, or obstruction.

Meckel's diverticulum with bleeding.description: A congenital ileal diverticulum that can harbor ectopic gastric mucosa, causing ulceration and lower GI bleeding; often presents in younger individuals but can be found in adults.

case: A 73-year-old man presented with abdominal distention and maldigestion for 1 month. The patient had a medical history of diabetes and hypertension. On physical examination, an intraabdominal mass was palpated in the epigastric area, and the patient did not complain of pain and tenderness. Laboratory findings showed no abnormalities except an elevated fasting glucose level.

diagnoses.name: Malignant gastrointestinal stromal tumor
diagnoses.icd11_title: Malignant GIST - [gastrointestinal stromal tumour] of large intestine

Pancreatic adenocarcinoma (body/tail).description: A malignant tumor of the exocrine pancreas; body/tail lesions often present late with vague symptoms and without jaundice.

Gastric carcinoma.description: Malignancy of the stomach that can present with early satiety, dyspepsia, weight loss, and sometimes a palpable epigastric mass in advanced disease.

Gastrointestinal stromal tumor (GIST) of.normalized_text: Gastrointestinal stromal tumor (GIST) of the stomach
Gastrointestinal stromal tumor (GIST) of.description: A mesenchymal tumor of the gastrointestinal tract, often arising in the stomach; may present as a painless, palpable mass or with bleeding.

Abdominal aortic aneurysm (AAA).description: Dilation of the abdominal aorta, typically in older men, which may present as a palpable, sometimes pulsatile, abdominal mass and is often asymptomatic.

Pancreatic cystic neoplasm (e.g., IPMN o.normalized_text: Pancreatic cystic neoplasm (e.g., IPMN or mucinous cystic neoplasm)
Pancreatic cystic neoplasm (e.g., IPMN o.description: Cystic lesions of the pancreas that can cause exocrine insufficiency and vague abdominal symptoms; may be incidentally found as a mass.

Intraabdominal lymphoma (e.g., non-Hodgk.description: Lymphoid malignancy that can present with painless abdominal mass and distention due to bulky mesenteric or retroperitoneal disease.

case: A 58-year-old overweight African American male presented with a 5-year history of a slightly pruritic and painful rash that worsened during summers, and blisters sometimes developed. Emollients were unhelpful. The patient was otherwise healthy, performed indoor manual labor as a maintenance engineer, and had no significant sun exposure. His sister had diabetes mellitus and a similar rash in her axillae. Physical examination revealed irregularly thickened skin containing hyperpigmentation, hypopigmentation, multiple acrochordons (skin tags), malodorous crust, and areas of maceration and erosion. Further examination showed pseudofolliculitis barbae in the submental and mandibular regions bilaterally. The nails, oral cavity, and mucosal membranes appeared normal.

Hailey-Hailey disease (benign familial c.description: A chronic, relapsing genetic acantholytic dermatosis affecting intertriginous areas, characterized by painful, pruritic erosions that worsen with heat, sweat, and friction; often has a family history.

Hidradenitis suppurativa.description: A chronic inflammatory disease of hair follicles in intertriginous areas characterized by painful nodules, abscesses, malodorous drainage, and scarring; exacerbated by friction, heat, and obesity.

Inverse (intertriginous) psoriasis.description: A form of psoriasis affecting skin folds, presenting as well-demarcated erythematous plaques that can become macerated and fissured; may be sore or pruritic and worsen with heat and moisture.

Candidal intertrigo (chronic/relapsing).description: Yeast overgrowth in skin folds causing erythematous, macerated, malodorous, pruritic patches with fissuring; often worsens in heat and humidity and may relapse if risk factors persist.

Acanthosis nigricans with skin tags (acr.normalized_text: Acanthosis nigricans with skin tags (acrochordons) due to insulin resistance
Acanthosis nigricans with skin tags (acr.description: A velvety hyperpigmented thickening of intertriginous skin associated with insulin resistance; commonly accompanied by multiple skin tags, especially in overweight individuals or those with diabetes risk.

case: A 22-year-old female presented with a gradually increasing pelvic mass with tenderness for 1 month. There was no evidence of previous trauma or fever, and no history of other medical or surgical disease and no evidence of pregnancy. On physical examination, there was a palpable mass with tenderness in her left pelvic area.

Functional ovarian cyst (follicular or c.normalized_text: Functional ovarian cyst (follicular or corpus luteum cyst)
Functional ovarian cyst (follicular or c.description: A benign, fluid-filled ovarian cyst arising from normal ovulatory processes; common in reproductive-age women and can enlarge over weeks and cause unilateral pelvic pain or a palpable mass.

Endometrioma (ovarian endometriosis cyst.description: A cyst formed by ectopic endometrial tissue on the ovary, often called a 'chocolate cyst'; typically presents with chronic pelvic pain and a tender adnexal mass, and may enlarge over time.

Mature cystic teratoma (dermoid cyst).description: A common benign ovarian germ cell tumor in young women; often asymptomatic but can present as a slowly enlarging adnexal mass and may cause pain if large or complicated.

Pedunculated subserosal uterine fibroid.description: A benign smooth muscle tumor of the uterus that can protrude on a stalk and present as a palpable pelvic mass; may cause localized tenderness, especially if degenerating or torsed.

Hydrosalpinx.description: A fluid-filled, dilated fallopian tube usually from prior salpingitis or obstruction; can present as a unilateral adnexal mass with chronic pelvic discomfort.

Tubo-ovarian abscess (TOA).description: A complex infectious mass involving the fallopian tube and ovary, typically a complication of pelvic inflammatory disease; often presents with pelvic pain, adnexal mass, and systemic signs.

Ovarian torsion.description: Twisting of the ovary/adnexa leading to venous congestion and ischemia; usually presents with acute severe unilateral pelvic pain and adnexal tenderness/mass, but can have subacute or intermittent symptoms if partial or intermittent torsion.

case: 36-year-old female with no past medical history who developed lower limbs and para-spinal muscle spasms that progressed over 3 months. Her symptoms continued to progress and she became wheelchair-bound 6 months later. When reviewed at institution, she was severely disabled requiring regular IVIG treatments at a dose of 90g every 12 days. She was taking regular diazepam at a dose of 30mg per day and morphine up to 60mg a day to control pain. On examination, she had brisk reflexes and severe clonus. The muscle spasms were severe enough to compromise her breathing and she required intermittent oxygen.

Stiff-person syndrome (stiff-person spec.normalized_text: Stiff-person syndrome (stiff-person spectrum disorder, anti-GAD65 related)
Stiff-person syndrome (stiff-person spec.description: An autoimmune neurologic disorder characterized by fluctuating axial and proximal limb stiffness and painful spasms, often associated with anti-GAD65 or amphiphysin antibodies. It frequently affects women and responds to GABAergic agents and immunotherapy such as IVIG.

Progressive encephalomyelitis with rigid.normalized_text: Progressive encephalomyelitis with rigidity and myoclonus (PERM), often anti-glycine receptor mediated
Progressive encephalomyelitis with rigid.description: A severe variant within the stiff-person spectrum featuring widespread rigidity, spasms, hyperreflexia/clonus, brainstem involvement, and autonomic features; frequently associated with anti-glycine receptor antibodies and often responsive to IVIG and benzodiazepines.

Hereditary spastic paraplegia (HSP).description: A group of genetic disorders characterized by slowly progressive lower-limb spasticity and weakness due to corticospinal tract degeneration; may be pure (spastic paraparesis) or complex (with additional neurologic features).

Primary lateral sclerosis (PLS) or other.normalized_text: Primary lateral sclerosis (PLS) or other pure upper motor neuron syndrome
Primary lateral sclerosis (PLS) or other.description: A degenerative upper motor neuron disorder characterized by slowly progressive spasticity, hyperreflexia, and clonus without lower motor neuron signs for several years.

Inflammatory/demyelinating myelopathy (e.normalized_text: Inflammatory/demyelinating myelopathy (e.g., transverse myelitis or multiple sclerosis-related myelopathy)
Inflammatory/demyelinating myelopathy (e.description: Immune-mediated spinal cord inflammation causing motor and sensory deficits with upper motor neuron signs; may occur as part of multiple sclerosis or as isolated transverse myelitis; typically treated with steroids, plasma exchange, or other immunotherapies.
