case: 46-year-old woman presented with frequent collapse. Medical history included carotid endarterectomy in 2005 following a small right hemispheric stroke, and hypercholesterolaemia. No previous dermatological or scalp problems. Current medications: clopidogrel 75mg, aspirin 80mg, and simvastatin 40mg daily.

Carotid sinus hypersensitivity.description: Exaggerated response to carotid sinus stimulation causing bradycardia, hypotension, and syncope; can be triggered by head turning, tight collars, or spontaneous in susceptible individuals. Prior neck surgery can be a risk factor.

Vasovagal syncope.description: The most common cause of fainting due to reflex-mediated hypotension and/or bradycardia, often triggered by pain, stress, or prolonged standing and typically with a prodrome.

Cardiac arrhythmia (e.g., bradyarrhythmi.description: Abnormal heart rhythms can cause transient cerebral hypoperfusion leading to abrupt syncope without warning; may be intermittent and recurrent.

Orthostatic hypotension.description: Drop in blood pressure upon standing causing dizziness or syncope; can be due to autonomic dysfunction, volume depletion, or medications.

Transient ischemic attacks (vertebrobasi.description: Transient episodes of cerebral ischemia affecting the posterior circulation can cause sudden falls or syncope-like events, sometimes without prominent focal deficits; risk increased with atherosclerosis.

Anemia from occult gastrointestinal blee.description: Chronic blood loss from the GI tract due to antiplatelet therapy can cause iron-deficiency anemia leading to fatigue, dizziness, and syncope.

case: 60-year-old woman with rheumatoid arthritis treated with methotrexate and adalimumab. Four months before admission, she developed pain and stiffness in the metacarpophalangeal and interphalangeal joints, right ankle, and both knees. Six weeks before admission, she had severe arthralgia, low-grade fever, livedo reticularis on the legs, and purpuric lesions around the malleoli. Labs then showed anemia, leukopenia, neutropenia, hypergammaglobulinemia, high rheumatoid factor, positive ANA, low C4, anti-dsDNA positivity, and positive cryoglobulins; HIV, hepatitis B, and hepatitis C tests were negative. On admission, she had fever and pancytopenia, without hepatosplenomegaly or lymphadenopathy. Blood, urine, and sputum cultures, chest/abdomen/pelvis CT, peripheral blood CMV PCR, and tuberculin skin test were negative.

Mixed cryoglobulinemic vasculitis (essen.description: Immune-complex mediated small-vessel vasculitis characterized by circulating cryoglobulins, often causing palpable purpura, arthralgias, livedo, peripheral neuropathy, and hypocomplementemia; commonly HCV-related but can be associated with autoimmune disease such as rheumatoid arthritis or triggered by biologics.

Anti-TNF-induced lupus (adalimumab-induc.description: A lupus-like syndrome triggered by TNF-alpha inhibitors characterized by new-onset autoantibodies (ANA, anti-dsDNA), hypocomplementemia, constitutional symptoms, serositis, rash, and cytopenias; improves with withdrawal of the drug.

Rheumatoid vasculitis.description: A severe extra-articular manifestation of long-standing, seropositive rheumatoid arthritis resulting in necrotizing small- to medium-vessel vasculitis with skin lesions (purpura, ulcers, livedo), peripheral neuropathy, and systemic symptoms.

Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) or RA.normalized_text: Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) or RA–SLE overlap (rhupus)
Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) or RA.description: An autoimmune disease with multisystem involvement; RA patients can develop overlapping SLE with characteristic ANA, anti-dsDNA, hypocomplementemia, cytopenias, fevers, and vasculitic or other cutaneous manifestations.

Felty syndrome.description: A triad of seropositive rheumatoid arthritis, neutropenia, and splenomegaly; predisposes to infections and can be associated with extra-articular RA features and vasculitic skin lesions.

Methotrexate-induced pancytopenia.description: Bone marrow suppression due to methotrexate leading to pancytopenia, often presenting with fever from neutropenia; risk increased with renal impairment, drug interactions, or folate deficiency.

Hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (seco.description: A life-threatening hyperinflammatory syndrome triggered by infection, malignancy, or autoimmune disease/therapy, characterized by persistent fever, cytopenias, and organ dysfunction; requires specific laboratory criteria (e.g., hyperferritinemia).

case: A 25-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes mellitus presented to the emergency department for evaluation of a hyperpigmented lesion on the shin. The lesion appeared as a small reddish-brown macule 3 years ago and has gradually increased in size. During the past several months, the lesion has become indented and increasingly tender. The patient denies systemic symptoms, including fevers and chills, and is primarily concerned about the changing appearance of the lesion and the new-onset tenderness. Laboratory evaluation shows a random blood glucose level of 217 mg/dL (12 mmol/L).

Necrobiosis lipoidica (diabeticorum).description: A chronic granulomatous skin disorder strongly associated with diabetes mellitus, characterized by yellow-brown atrophic plaques with telangiectasias and indurated borders, most often on the anterior shins. Lesions may become tender and ulcerate.

Diabetic dermopathy (shin spots).description: Common cutaneous manifestation of diabetes presenting as multiple, small, atrophic, hyperpigmented macules on the shins. Lesions are usually asymptomatic and stable after initial appearance.

Dermatofibroma.description: A benign fibrohistiocytic skin nodule, often on the lower legs of young women, presenting as a firm hyperpigmented papule that dimples with lateral compression; may be mildly tender.

Cutaneous melanoma.description: A malignant tumor of melanocytes that presents as an evolving pigmented lesion with asymmetry, border irregularity, color variegation, diameter enlargement, or evolving symptoms (ABCDE). Can occur on the lower extremities in women.

Granuloma annulare.description: A benign inflammatory dermatosis, often in young women, characterized by annular plaques with central clearing that may appear depressed; commonly on extremities and sometimes associated with diabetes.

case: 14-year-old boy with acute fear of choking when swallowing սկս 2 days after choking on chicken at dinner, followed by vomiting with attempted eating, markedly reduced oral intake, drooling, dry mouth, and fatigue/somnolence. Mother also reported episodes of inspiratory stridor during sleep over the preceding few weeks. Past history includes infantile gastroesophageal reflux, milk-protein allergy, sensory-integration training, keratosis pilaris, and eczema; no medications. Exam showed an alert, anxious-appearing boy with persistent involuntary burping, drooling, dry oral mucosa, normal neurologic exam, and later hypertonic leg muscles with a mildly positive left Chvostek sign.

Eosinophilic esophagitis with acute food.normalized_text: Eosinophilic esophagitis with acute food bolus impaction
Eosinophilic esophagitis with acute food.description: Chronic, immune-mediated esophageal disease often associated with atopy that can present with dysphagia and food impaction, especially with meats like chicken.

Esophageal foreign body impaction.description: Retention of a swallowed food bolus or object in the esophagus causing obstruction, drooling, and inability to tolerate oral intake.

Phagophobia (post-choking psychogenic dy.description: Avoidant Restrictive Food Intake Disorder variant where a traumatic choking event leads to fear of swallowing, avoidance of eating, and secondary weight or intake issues.

Laryngopharyngeal reflux (GERD-related l.description: Reflux of gastric contents to the larynx/pharynx causing laryngeal irritation, laryngospasm, and sometimes nocturnal stridor.

Hypocalcemia with tetany due to hyperven.normalized_text: Hypocalcemia with tetany due to hyperventilation (respiratory alkalosis) from panic
Hypocalcemia with tetany due to hyperven.description: Panic-induced hyperventilation can cause respiratory alkalosis leading to decreased ionized calcium and neuromuscular excitability (tetany).

Vocal cord dysfunction (paradoxical voca.normalized_text: Vocal cord dysfunction (paradoxical vocal fold motion)
Vocal cord dysfunction (paradoxical voca.description: Intermittent inappropriate adduction of the vocal cords during inspiration causing stridor and dyspnea, often associated with anxiety and irritants like reflux.

Achalasia (pediatric).description: Esophageal motility disorder with failure of lower esophageal sphincter relaxation and aperistalsis, causing progressive dysphagia and regurgitation; rare in adolescents.

case: 57-year-old woman with resected stage IIIC cutaneous melanoma presented with fever. Four months before admission, she developed bleeding from a scalp lesion; evaluation showed ulcerated melanoma with positive margins. Three months before admission, she underwent wide local excision and neck lymph-node dissection, which showed metastatic melanoma in 2 of 26 lymph nodes; BRAF V600E mutation was identified. One month before admission, she started adjuvant dabrafenib and trametinib, after which fever and nausea began within 1 day, resolving after temporary discontinuation and antipyretics. Fever recurred 2 weeks before admission. On presentation, temperature was 40.2°C, pulse 108 beats per minute, blood pressure 85/53 mm Hg, and oxygen saturation 94% on room air; she was diaphoretic, ill appearing, and had mild right upper quadrant tenderness, without rash.

Dabrafenib/Trametinib-induced pyrexia sy.description: A common adverse effect of combined BRAF and MEK inhibition characterized by high fevers, chills, malaise, hypotension, and constitutional symptoms; often occurs early after treatment initiation, may recur with rechallenge, and can be accompanied by transient hepatic enzyme elevations.

Sepsis of unclear source (bacterial).description: Systemic inflammatory response to infection causing fever, tachycardia, hypotension, and potential end-organ dysfunction; common sources include biliary, urinary, pulmonary, and skin/soft tissue.

Acute cholecystitis (including acalculou.description: Inflammation of the gallbladder, often due to cystic duct obstruction (calculous) or occurring without stones in systemic illness (acalculous); presents with fever, right upper quadrant pain/tenderness, and can lead to sepsis.

Drug-induced liver injury (DILI) from da.description: Hepatotoxicity due to BRAF/MEK inhibitors can cause transaminitis or cholestatic injury; patients may develop right upper quadrant discomfort, nausea, and low-grade fever; severe cases can cause systemic symptoms.

Hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (HLH).description: A hyperinflammatory syndrome characterized by persistent high fevers, cytopenias, hepatosplenomegaly, and elevated ferritin; can be triggered by malignancy or drugs and may mimic sepsis.

case: 59-year-old man with history of prostate cancer metastatic to lumbar spine and periaortic lymph nodes diagnosed in 2001, with initial PSA of 11.3 ng/mL. In August 2011, presented to emergency room with abdominal pain. Lab tests showed elevated lipase (874 U/L), alkaline phosphatase (289 IU/L), and ALT (222 IU/L), with normal bilirubin. Later returned with right upper quadrant abdominal pain, tachycardia but afebrile. Physical exam showed positive Murphy's sign and palpable gallbladder. Labs showed elevated alkaline phosphatase of 357 IU/L and normal serum lipase.

Acute calculous cholecystitis.description: Inflammation of the gallbladder due to cystic duct obstruction by a gallstone, leading to RUQ pain and systemic inflammatory response.

Gallstone pancreatitis (biliary pancreat.description: Acute pancreatitis triggered by transient obstruction of the ampulla by a gallstone, often accompanied by elevated pancreatic enzymes and cholestatic liver tests.

Choledocholithiasis (common bile duct st.description: Presence of a gallstone in the common bile duct causing biliary obstruction and cholestatic liver enzyme abnormalities.

Acute cholangitis.description: Bacterial infection of the biliary tree due to obstruction, typically presenting with RUQ pain, fever, and jaundice (Charcot triad).

Acalculous cholecystitis.description: Inflammation of the gallbladder without gallstones, often in critically ill or debilitated patients, due to gallbladder stasis and ischemia.

case: 13-year-old Caucasian boy with progressive symptoms including Addison’s disease, dysphagia, muscle weakness, excessive fatigue, and recent gait ataxia. He was born after an uneventful term pregnancy and had bilateral cryptorchidism, inguinal hernia, and hypospadias at birth. Early development was initially normal, but global developmental delay and mild intellectual disability were later recognized. He had deficient tear production since infancy. At age 2, he developed recurrent vomiting, failure to thrive, and progressive skin pigmentation. At age 4, he had recurrent hypotonia, hypoglycemia, and hypothermia, leading to diagnosis of Addison’s disease. Progressive dysphagia began at age 11 and later prevented normal swallowing without liquids. Examination showed severe hyperpigmentation and hyperkeratosis of the elbows and knuckles, facial dysmorphism, dysarthria, nasal speech, saccadic eye movements with horizontal gaze nystagmus, bilateral dilated pupils with poor light response, mild bilateral optic atrophy, distal arm weakness and wasting, milder leg weakness, unsteady gait, hyperreflexia, and bilateral extensor plantar responses. Laboratory studies showed markedly elevated ACTH with normal electrolytes, aldosterone, and renin, consistent with isolated glucocorticoid deficiency.

Allgrove (Triple-A/4A) syndrome.description: A rare autosomal recessive ACTH-resistance disorder caused by AAAS gene variants, classically characterized by alacrima, achalasia, and adrenal insufficiency; many patients develop progressive neurologic/autonomic features (4A).

X-linked adrenoleukodystrophy (cerebral.description: A peroxisomal disorder due to ABCD1 mutations causing very-long-chain fatty acid accumulation; presents in boys with adrenal insufficiency and progressive demyelinating neurologic disease.

Familial glucocorticoid deficiency (ACTH.normalized_text: Familial glucocorticoid deficiency (ACTH resistance, MC2R/MRAP variants)
Familial glucocorticoid deficiency (ACTH.description: An autosomal recessive disorder of ACTH receptor signaling causing isolated glucocorticoid deficiency with preserved mineralocorticoid function.

X-linked congenital adrenal hypoplasia (.description: A developmental disorder of the adrenal cortex leading to primary adrenal insufficiency in infancy/childhood and hypogonadotropic hypogonadism; may be associated with cryptorchidism and genital anomalies.

Hereditary sensory and autonomic neuropa.normalized_text: Hereditary sensory and autonomic neuropathy type III (familial dysautonomia)
Hereditary sensory and autonomic neuropa.description: An autosomal recessive disorder (ELP1/IKBKAP) characterized by widespread autonomic and sensory dysfunction with alacrima, GI dysmotility, and neurologic abnormalities; most common in individuals of Ashkenazi Jewish descent.

Mitochondrial leukodystrophy/mitochondri.normalized_text: Mitochondrial leukodystrophy/mitochondrial encephalopathy with secondary adrenal involvement
Mitochondrial leukodystrophy/mitochondri.description: A group of disorders involving mitochondrial dysfunction leading to progressive neurologic decline, ataxia, optic involvement, and sometimes endocrine abnormalities including adrenal insufficiency.

case: 55-year-old woman with a 13-year history of invasive ductal carcinoma of the right breast, now stage IV with metastases to bone, lungs, and liver. She had prior mastectomy, multiple systemic therapies, and stem-cell transplantation 8 years earlier; most recent treatment was anastrozole for 3 months and paracetamol for pain. She developed progressive generalized weakness and episodic confusion over several days, rapidly worsening to unresponsiveness. On admission, she was found disoriented on the floor with lower leg weakness and inability to follow basic instructions. Examination showed she was awake but unresponsive and uncooperative, without focal neurologic deficits initially; vital signs were normal except for mild tachycardia, and she was afebrile. Baseline brain MRI 2 weeks earlier was normal.

Hypercalcemia of malignancy.description: Elevated serum calcium due to tumor-related factors (e.g., PTHrP secretion or bone metastases) causing neuromuscular and CNS dysfunction.

Hepatic encephalopathy due to liver meta.normalized_text: Hepatic encephalopathy due to liver metastases
Hepatic encephalopathy due to liver meta.description: Neuropsychiatric dysfunction from impaired hepatic detoxification and elevated ammonia, often triggered by acute hepatic decompensation.

Leptomeningeal carcinomatosis.description: Dissemination of malignant cells to the leptomeninges causing multifocal neurologic dysfunction and altered mental status; can be missed on early imaging.

Nonconvulsive status epilepticus.description: Ongoing seizure activity without overt convulsions leading to altered consciousness and unresponsiveness; often precipitated by structural or metabolic disease.

Sepsis-associated encephalopathy.description: Diffuse brain dysfunction due to systemic infection and inflammatory response without direct CNS infection; can present without fever in immunocompromised patients.

Paraneoplastic limbic encephalitis.description: Immune-mediated inflammation of limbic structures associated with cancer (including breast), causing subacute cognitive changes, confusion, and behavioral disturbances.

Hyponatremia due to SIADH.description: Syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion leading to low serum sodium and cerebral edema, often causing confusion and lethargy in cancer patients.

case: 54-year-old woman with no significant past medical history presented with 1 month of progressive four-extremity weakness, sensory changes, and subsequent urinary difficulty. Examination showed hyperreflexia, positive Babinski sign, bilateral Hoffmann and Tromner signs, and asymmetric weakness (MRC 2/5 on the right, 4/5 on the left). Sensory loss included decreased pinprick and temperature below the C4 level, worse on the left, and decreased vibration and proprioception, worse on the right. Serologic autoimmune studies and cerebrospinal fluid analysis were normal; angiotensin converting enzyme was mildly elevated. Brain MRI, chest and abdominal CT, and nerve conduction study showed no abnormalities.

Cervical spinal cord meningioma (intradu.normalized_text: Cervical spinal cord meningioma (intradural extramedullary tumor) causing Brown-Séquard syndrome
Cervical spinal cord meningioma (intradu.description: A benign dural-based tumor compressing the cervical cord; commonly presents in middle-aged women with progressive myelopathy and often a Brown-Séquard pattern due to hemicord compression.

Cervical disc herniation/osteophyte with.normalized_text: Cervical disc herniation/osteophyte with compressive myelopathy (Brown-Séquard pattern)
Cervical disc herniation/osteophyte with.description: A focal cervical disc protrusion or osteophytic spur causing hemicord compression and myelopathy, which can produce a Brown-Séquard syndrome.

Idiopathic acute transverse myelitis.description: An inflammatory demyelinating disorder of the spinal cord causing a sensory level, motor and autonomic dysfunction, typically evolving over days to weeks.

Multiple sclerosis (isolated cervical co.normalized_text: Multiple sclerosis (isolated cervical cord demyelinating plaque)
Multiple sclerosis (isolated cervical co.description: A demyelinating disease of the central nervous system that can present with a focal spinal cord lesion causing myelopathy; sometimes brain MRI can be normal early.

Neurosarcoidosis involving the spinal co.description: Granulomatous inflammation of the central nervous system due to sarcoidosis; can cause myelopathy with or without systemic disease.

Spinal dural arteriovenous fistula (SDAV.description: An acquired shunt between dural arteries and veins causing venous congestion of the spinal cord, leading to progressive myelopathy and sphincter dysfunction.

Cervical syringomyelia/syringobulbia.description: A fluid-filled cavity within the cervical spinal cord disrupting decussating spinothalamic fibers and possibly corticospinal tracts, causing dissociated sensory loss and myelopathy.

case: 33-year-old male with a 20-day history of cough with small amounts of yellow-white sticky sputum, starting after a cold. He denied hemoptysis, fever, chills, chest pain, and dyspnea initially. He received unspecified intravenous treatment at a local clinic without improvement. Seven days before admission, the cough worsened, especially at night causing sleep disturbance, and was sometimes accompanied by right-sided chest pain. Past history was unremarkable; he smoked about 10 cigarettes/day for over 10 years and did not drink alcohol. Physical examination showed T 36.2℃, pulse 112/min, respiration 19/min, BP 126/85 mmHg; symmetric chest, equal respiratory movement and vocal fremitus, clear percussion notes, coarse breath sounds bilaterally, and a small amount of wet rales in the right lung.

Acute bronchitis.description: Acute inflammation of the bronchi, most often viral, causing cough and sputum production following an upper respiratory infection. Usually self-limited over 1–3 weeks.

Community-acquired pneumonia (atypical,.description: Lower respiratory tract infection that may present subacutely with prominent cough and few systemic signs. Atypical pathogens can cause mild fever or none and modest auscultatory findings.

Post-infectious (post-viral) cough.description: Prolonged cough lasting up to 8 weeks after an upper respiratory infection due to airway inflammation and heightened cough reflex without ongoing infection.

Cough-variant asthma.description: Asthma phenotype where chronic cough is the predominant or only symptom, often worse at night and following viral infections; airway hyperresponsiveness without classic wheezing.

Upper airway cough syndrome (postnasal d.description: Chronic cough due to nasal/sinus pathology with posterior drainage stimulating cough receptors; often follows a cold and is worse at night.

Pulmonary tuberculosis.description: Chronic infectious disease caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis, typically presenting with cough over weeks, constitutional symptoms, and possibly focal chest findings.

case: A 64-year-old male patient from Smoljanci, Istria presented with firm, migrating nodules in the brachial region without history of serious disease. He had no travel outside Croatia but spent recreational time in forests and islands near his residence and owned a pet dog. Physical examination revealed a painless, well-demarcated subcutaneous nodule in his right upper arm measuring 1.5 × 1.5 × 1.0 cm. Ultrasonographic findings of the nodule appeared normal. Laboratory tests showed total blood counts, erythrocyte sedimentation rate and C-reactive protein within normal values. Serologic results for trichinosis, toxocariasis, schistosomiasis, distomatosis and cysticercosis were negative.

Subcutaneous dirofilariasis (Dirofilaria.description: Zoonotic filarial infection transmitted by mosquitoes from dogs; common in Mediterranean Europe. In humans it typically causes solitary or migrating painless subcutaneous nodules, often in the head, neck, or upper extremities, with minimal systemic inflammation.

Sparganosis (Spirometra spp. larval infe.description: Infection by plerocercoid larvae of Spirometra acquired via contaminated water or undercooked amphibians/reptiles; causes migrating subcutaneous nodules, sometimes with eosinophilia.

Lipoma.description: A benign tumor of mature adipose tissue presenting as a soft, mobile, subcutaneous mass that is usually painless and slow-growing.

Epidermoid (epidermal inclusion) cyst.description: A benign cyst arising from the epidermis or hair follicle infundibulum, often presenting as a firm, well-circumscribed subcutaneous nodule; may have a central punctum and can become inflamed.

Gnathostomiasis (Gnathostoma spp.).description: Zoonotic nematode infection acquired by ingesting raw/undercooked fish or contaminated water; causes intermittent, migrating subcutaneous swellings and eosinophilia; more common in Asia and Latin America.

Nodular fasciitis.description: A benign, rapidly growing myofibroblastic proliferation in the subcutis or fascia; presents as a firm nodule, often on the upper extremities; can be mistaken for sarcoma but is self-limited.

case: 66-year-old man with progressive gait instability and frequent falls since around 2000, followed by blurred vision, photophobia, and worsening imbalance from 2003. He had bilateral cataract surgery with lens implantation in 2000 without benefit. Over time he developed slurred speech, inability to look down, dysphagia with repeated aspirations, and increasing postural instability requiring a cane. On examination he had irregular pupils with sluggish light reflexes, severe impairment of voluntary vertical gaze, slowed horizontal pursuit with bilateral adduction paresis, preserved convergence early on, later absent vertical and medial eye movements, no Bell’s phenomenon, no optokinetic or caloric-induced nystagmus, and absent doll’s eye movements. He also had severe nuchal rigidity, retrocollis, axial rigidity, inability to sit independently, backward falls, and no resting tremor.

Progressive supranuclear palsy (Richards.description: A neurodegenerative tauopathy characterized by early postural instability with backward falls, axial rigidity, dysarthria/dysphagia, and a supranuclear vertical gaze palsy due to midbrain dysfunction.

Parkinson’s disease (akinetic-rigid pred.description: A synucleinopathy presenting with bradykinesia, rigidity, tremor, and postural instability; typical ocular movements are preserved except for hypometric saccades in later stages.

Multiple system atrophy, parkinsonian ty.description: A rapidly progressive synucleinopathy with parkinsonism poorly responsive to levodopa, autonomic failure, and sometimes cerebellar signs; ocular findings typically include saccadic abnormalities but not marked vertical supranuclear palsy.

Corticobasal degeneration/corticobasal s.description: A neurodegenerative tauopathy with asymmetric parkinsonism, limb apraxia, dystonia, myoclonus, and cortical signs; ocular motor abnormalities can occur but profound vertical supranuclear gaze palsy is less typical than in PSP.

Dorsal midbrain (Parinaud) syndrome due.normalized_text: Dorsal midbrain (Parinaud) syndrome due to structural midbrain pathology
Dorsal midbrain (Parinaud) syndrome due.description: A syndrome from lesions of the dorsal midbrain (e.g., tumor, stroke, MS) causing vertical gaze palsy, light-near dissociation of pupils, and convergence abnormalities.

case: A 36-year-old man, sexually active with men, presented to the emergency department with a 2-week history of fever, headache, drowsiness, and photophobia. He was previously healthy. Physical examination revealed a temperature of 38.3°C and neck stiffness. CT of the head was normal. Lumbar puncture showed an opening pressure of 29 cm of water (ref: <20 cm). CSF analysis revealed: cell count 340 cells/µL (90% mononuclear cells, predominantly lymphocytes), glucose 46 mg/dL, and protein 0.80 g/L. HIV antibody test was positive with viral load 300,000 copies/mL and CD4+ count of 7 cells/µL.

Cryptococcal meningitis (Cryptococcus ne.description: An opportunistic fungal infection causing subacute to chronic meningitis, classically in patients with advanced AIDS; characterized by high opening pressure and lymphocytic CSF.

Tuberculous meningitis.description: Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection of the meninges causing subacute meningitis; common in immunocompromised patients; often shows lymphocytic CSF with high protein and low glucose.

HSV-2 lymphocytic meningitis.description: Herpes simplex virus type 2 can cause a benign recurrent or primary aseptic meningitis with lymphocytic CSF, typically in sexually active adults.

Coccidioidal meningitis.description: Meningeal infection by Coccidioides species, a dimorphic fungus endemic to the southwestern United States; causes chronic basilar meningitis with lymphocytic CSF, very high protein, low glucose, and elevated opening pressure, especially in immunocompromised hosts.

Cytomegalovirus (CMV) meningoencephaliti.description: An opportunistic infection in advanced AIDS (CD4 <50) causing encephalitis or ventriculoencephalitis; CSF may show lymphocytic pleocytosis and elevated protein.

case: An 83-year-old woman presented to the acute stroke unit with sudden onset double vision that had lasted for three hours. She had a medical history of monoclonal gammopathy of uncertain significance and atrial fibrillation, for which she was not receiving anticoagulation because of an adverse reaction to warfarin. She had no history of transient ischaemic attack or stroke. She had diplopia only when looking through her right eye. On examination, she was unable to adduct her left eye, with nystagmus in her right eye when she attempted to do this. Her neurological examination was otherwise normal.

Internuclear ophthalmoplegia (INO) due t.normalized_text: Internuclear ophthalmoplegia (INO) due to ischemic stroke (medial longitudinal fasciculus infarct)
Internuclear ophthalmoplegia (INO) due t.description: A brainstem disorder caused by a lesion of the medial longitudinal fasciculus, most commonly due to small ischemic infarcts in older adults, leading to impaired adduction of the ipsilesional eye with abducting nystagmus of the contralateral eye and binocular diplopia.

Posterior circulation ischemic stroke (p.description: An acute ischemic event in the vertebrobasilar territory affecting brainstem structures, which can produce isolated ocular motor abnormalities such as INO with minimal additional deficits.

Ischemic oculomotor (cranial nerve III).description: Microvascular ischemia of the oculomotor nerve, often due to vascular risk factors, leading to deficits in adduction, elevation, and depression, sometimes with ptosis and pupil sparing.

Ocular myasthenia gravis.description: An autoimmune neuromuscular junction disorder that can present with fluctuating diplopia and ptosis due to extraocular muscle weakness; can mimic various ocular motor palsies.

Monocular diplopia from ocular causes (e.normalized_text: Monocular diplopia from ocular causes (e.g., corneal irregularity, cataract, high astigmatism) in the right eye
Monocular diplopia from ocular causes (e.description: Optical abnormalities of the cornea, lens, or tear film can cause double vision in one eye (monocular diplopia), often described as ghosting or multiple images, and persist when the affected eye is used alone.

Multiple sclerosis with internuclear oph.description: A demyelinating disease of the central nervous system that frequently affects the medial longitudinal fasciculus, causing INO, classically in younger adults and often bilateral, with variable onset and progression.

case: 35-day-old male infant with 2 days of progressive illness: initially well at a routine exam, then developed fussiness, pallor/warm skin, vomiting, fever, tachycardia, mottled skin, and respiratory distress on admission. Born at 37.5 weeks as a fraternal twin by cesarean section for breech presentation; previously healthy and fed breast milk plus formula. On exam he was febrile (39.1°C), pale, listless, fussy, tachycardic, tachypneic with retractions, and had mottled, slightly cool extremities, a grade 2/6 holosystolic-flow murmur, and splenomegaly 2–3 cm below the costal margin. Urinalysis showed dark red, cloudy urine with blood, protein, and granular casts.

Neonatal sepsis due to urinary tract inf.normalized_text: Neonatal sepsis due to urinary tract infection/pyelonephritis
Neonatal sepsis due to urinary tract inf.description: Serious bacterial infection in young infants commonly arising from the urinary tract, leading to bacteremia/sepsis and systemic inflammatory response with potential renal involvement.

Infective endocarditis with secondary gl.description: Infection of the endocardial surface (often on congenital lesions like VSD) causing systemic sepsis; immune complex deposition can lead to hematuria/proteinuria and renal casts; splenomegaly is common.

Atypical hemolytic uremic syndrome (comp.description: Complement dysregulation leading to thrombotic microangiopathy with microangiopathic hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia, and acute kidney injury; can present in infants without diarrhea.

Septic shock with acute tubular necrosis.normalized_text: Septic shock with acute tubular necrosis
Septic shock with acute tubular necrosis.description: Systemic infection causing circulatory collapse and multiorgan dysfunction; renal hypoperfusion and inflammatory injury lead to acute tubular necrosis with hematuria/proteinuria and granular casts.

Viral myocarditis with cardiogenic shock.description: Inflammation of the myocardium causing impaired cardiac function, leading to tachycardia, respiratory distress, poor perfusion; functional regurgitant murmurs may be present.

case: 70-year-old man with history of Gleason 9 (4+5) adenocarcinoma treated with radical prostatectomy 10 years ago. Presented to primary care with rectal pain persisting for several weeks. Patient had lost 20 lbs over 3-4 weeks and complained of progressive fatigue, poor appetite, severe tenesmus, and rectal pain. Patient had been living independently on West Coast but relocated to East Coast to be closer to adult children.

Rectal adenocarcinoma.description: Malignancy arising from the rectal mucosa, often presenting with obstructive or irritative rectal symptoms and constitutional signs.

Local recurrence or metastatic prostate.normalized_text: Local recurrence or metastatic prostate cancer with rectal involvement
Local recurrence or metastatic prostate.description: Recurrent prostate adenocarcinoma (despite prior radical prostatectomy) that invades or compresses the rectum, causing anorectal symptoms and systemic effects.

Anal squamous cell carcinoma.description: Cancer of the anal canal, commonly associated with HPV, presenting with anal/rectal pain, tenesmus, and sometimes constitutional symptoms.

Ulcerative proctitis (inflammatory bowel.normalized_text: Ulcerative proctitis (inflammatory bowel disease limited to the rectum)
Ulcerative proctitis (inflammatory bowel.description: Inflammatory bowel disease confined to the rectum causing rectal urgency, tenesmus, and pain.

Infectious proctitis.description: Infection of the rectal mucosa (bacterial, viral, or parasitic), often sexually transmitted, causing rectal pain, urgency, and tenesmus.

Perirectal abscess.description: Infection leading to a collection of pus adjacent to the rectum or anal canal, causing severe pain and tenesmus.

Anal fissure or severe hemorrhoidal dise.normalized_text: Anal fissure or severe hemorrhoidal disease
Anal fissure or severe hemorrhoidal dise.description: Benign anorectal conditions that can cause pain with defecation and irritative rectal symptoms.

case: 27-year-old man with 3 days of progressive myalgias in the thighs followed by acute weakness of the legs and arms on the day of presentation, unable to lift his legs or stand. For several months he had insomnia, loose stools, ~5 kg weight loss, and hand tremor. He started an herbal supplement 4 days before presentation. On exam: bilateral conjunctival injection, upper extremity strength 4/5, lower extremity strength 3/5, brisk patellar reflexes, and fine hand tremor. Labs showed severe hypokalemia (K 1.8 mmol/L), mild transaminitis, elevated alkaline phosphatase and bilirubin, mildly elevated CK and aldolase, and venous pH 7.29.

Thyrotoxic periodic paralysis.description: Acute, reversible hypokalemic paralysis due to intracellular potassium shift triggered by thyrotoxicosis; typically affects young men and can be precipitated by stress, high carbohydrate intake, or exogenous thyroid hormone.

Graves disease with hyperthyroid myopath.description: Autoimmune hyperthyroidism causing systemic hypermetabolic symptoms and a proximal myopathy characterized by muscle weakness and fatigue.

Hypokalemic paralysis due to gastrointes.normalized_text: Hypokalemic paralysis due to gastrointestinal potassium losses (diarrhea-related)
Hypokalemic paralysis due to gastrointes.description: Acute or subacute muscle weakness from total body potassium depletion caused by chronic diarrhea, often accompanied by normal anion gap metabolic acidosis.

Familial hypokalemic periodic paralysis.description: Inherited channelopathy causing episodic hypokalemia and flaccid paralysis, often triggered by rest after exercise or high-carbohydrate meals.

Guillain-Barré syndrome (acute inflammat.description: Immune-mediated polyradiculoneuropathy causing rapidly progressive, symmetric weakness, typically with areflexia and possible sensory symptoms.

Drug-induced liver injury from herbal su.normalized_text: Drug-induced liver injury from herbal supplement
Drug-induced liver injury from herbal su.description: Hepatotoxicity caused by herbal or dietary supplements, which can produce cholestatic or hepatocellular enzyme elevations and systemic symptoms.

case: A 70-year-old woman presented to the clinic for a routine examination. The patient reported that this mass had been present since birth. Her symptoms were minimal, with occasional difficulty cleaning the area and halitosis from entrapped food, but she was otherwise asymptomatic regarding the lesion.

Fissured tongue (lingua plicata).description: A benign condition characterized by grooves/fissures on the dorsal tongue, often congenital or appearing in childhood. Food can become trapped in fissures, causing halitosis and difficulty with hygiene.

Second branchial cleft anomaly with inte.normalized_text: Second branchial cleft anomaly with internal sinus (tonsillar fossa opening)
Second branchial cleft anomaly with inte.description: A congenital epithelial-lined tract or sinus from a second branchial cleft remnant that may open internally into the tonsillar fossa, potentially trapping food and causing halitosis; often minimally symptomatic unless infected.

Torus palatinus (or torus mandibularis).description: A benign bony exostosis of the hard palate (or lingual mandible) that is usually asymptomatic but can lead to food entrapment and hygiene difficulties when large.

Oral cavity lymphatic malformation (lymp.description: A congenital malformation of lymphatic vessels, often involving the tongue or oral mucosa; may present as a soft mass from birth and can harbor debris in surface pits, potentially causing halitosis.

Dermoid cyst of the floor of mouth/subme.normalized_text: Dermoid cyst of the floor of mouth/submental region
Dermoid cyst of the floor of mouth/subme.description: A congenital inclusion cyst containing skin adnexal elements; typically a midline, slow-growing mass that may be present from birth and often asymptomatic unless large.

case: A 52-year-old woman presented with a two-day history of lower back pain radiating into her left leg with associated leg weakness. She had a history of chronic back pain. Neurological examination revealed reduced power in her left leg (3/5), but was otherwise normal.

diagnoses.name: Intervertebral disc prolapse
diagnoses.icd11_title: Intervertebral disc degeneration without prolapsed disc with determinant

Lumbar intervertebral disc herniation wi.normalized_text: Lumbar intervertebral disc herniation with radiculopathy (sciatica)
Lumbar intervertebral disc herniation wi.description: Protrusion of a lumbar disc compresses a nerve root, causing radicular pain and possible motor weakness along the affected dermatome/myotome.

Lumbar spinal stenosis (degenerative).description: Narrowing of the lumbar spinal canal or foramina due to degenerative changes, leading to nerve root compression and neurogenic symptoms.

Cauda equina syndrome.description: Compression of the cauda equina nerves, often from a large herniated disc, causing severe back pain with bilateral radicular symptoms, motor deficits, and possible bowel/bladder or saddle sensory changes.

Piriformis syndrome (sciatic nerve entra.description: Compression or irritation of the sciatic nerve by the piriformis muscle, leading to buttock pain radiating down the leg, sometimes mimicking radiculopathy.

Spinal epidural abscess (lumbar).description: Infection in the epidural space causing inflammation and potential compression of neural elements; classically presents with back pain, fever, and neurological deficits.

Vertebral neoplasm with nerve root compr.normalized_text: Vertebral neoplasm with nerve root compression (metastatic or primary)
Vertebral neoplasm with nerve root compr.description: Tumor involving the vertebral column or foramina can compress nerve roots, causing radicular pain and focal neurological deficits.

case: A 52-year-old Korean man presented with a 1-month history of general weakness that was aggravated three days before his emergency room visit. Initial neurologic examination revealed disorientation of time, place, and person, attention deficit, immediate memory disturbance, dysarthria, weakness of bilateral upper extremities with increased deep tendon reflexes, and right hemiparetic gait. Blood work showed an elevated eosinophil count of 5,500/μL, representing 41% of total white blood cells. The patient's clinical history and basic examinations did not reveal any identifiable cause of hypereosinophilia, including parasitic infection, neoplasm, vasculitis, or allergy. Additionally, the patient had no prior clinical symptoms or signs suggesting Churg-Strauss syndrome, such as sinusitis or asthma. Cardiac enzymes were elevated with creatine kinase-MB at 7.3 ng/ml and troponin-I at 4.78 ng/ml. An echocardiogram revealed mild left ventricular inferior wall hypokinesia.

Hypereosinophilic syndrome (HES) with CN.normalized_text: Hypereosinophilic syndrome (HES) with CNS and cardiac involvement
Hypereosinophilic syndrome (HES) with CN.description: A group of disorders characterized by persistent marked eosinophilia leading to end-organ damage; common targets include heart, nervous system, skin, and lungs. Can be idiopathic or due to clonal/myeloproliferative variants.

Eosinophilic myocarditis (including Löff.description: Inflammatory myocardial disease driven by eosinophilic infiltration, often within the spectrum of HES; can cause myocardial injury, regional wall motion abnormalities, and predispose to mural thrombus and embolic events.

Ischemic stroke secondary to hypereosino.normalized_text: Ischemic stroke secondary to hypereosinophilia-associated thromboembolism
Ischemic stroke secondary to hypereosino.description: Hypereosinophilia can cause endothelial injury, hypercoagulability, and endomyocardial damage with mural thrombus formation, leading to cerebral emboli and ischemic strokes.

Eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyang.normalized_text: Eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis (EGPA, Churg-Strauss) – atypical/limited form
Eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyang.description: ANCA-associated eosinophilic small-vessel vasculitis featuring asthma, rhinosinusitis, eosinophilia, and multi-organ involvement including neuropathy and cardiomyopathy; CNS involvement is less common than peripheral neuropathy.

Drug reaction with eosinophilia and syst.normalized_text: Drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms (DRESS) with cardiac involvement
Drug reaction with eosinophilia and syst.description: A severe drug-induced hypersensitivity reaction characterized by eosinophilia and systemic organ involvement, commonly presenting with rash, fever, lymphadenopathy, and hepatitis; myocarditis can occur.

case: A 44-year-old woman with a history of breast cancer presented with abnormal findings on 18-fluorodeoxyglucose positron emission tomography imaging. She had previously been diagnosed with breast cancer (T1N2M0, Stage IIIa, intraductal carcinoma, triple negative cancer) and had undergone adjuvant chemotherapy and radiation therapy after a right breast conserving surgery 2 years prior. She was a non-smoker with no specific occupational or environmental exposure to known carcinogens and had been taking tamoxifen after chemotherapy. Laboratory results revealed mild anemia (hemoglobin 11.4 mg/dL) and leucopenia (3,300/μL), with all other results within normal limits. Additional laboratory findings included an elevated angiotensin I-converting enzyme level of 101 U/L, and her purified protein derivative skin test for tuberculosis was negative. The biopsy sample was also negative for tuberculosis antigen-specific interferon gamma.

Sarcoidosis.description: A multisystem granulomatous disease of unclear etiology characterized by noncaseating granulomas, most commonly affecting intrathoracic lymph nodes and lungs; often shows increased FDG uptake and elevated ACE levels.

Sarcoid-like reaction associated with ma.normalized_text: Sarcoid-like reaction associated with malignancy or therapy
Sarcoid-like reaction associated with ma.description: Noncaseating granulomatous reactions occurring in association with malignancies or as a reaction to cancer therapies; can mimic sarcoidosis clinically and radiographically.

Recurrent/metastatic breast cancer.description: Return or spread of breast carcinoma to regional nodes or distant sites; triple-negative cancers have higher recurrence risk and can show intense FDG uptake on PET imaging.

Lymphoma (Hodgkin or non-Hodgkin).description: Malignancy of lymphoid tissue often presenting with FDG-avid lymphadenopathy; can cause cytopenias if bone marrow or systemic involvement occurs.

Granulomatous fungal infection (e.g., hi.description: Infection by dimorphic fungi that can cause granulomatous inflammation and FDG-avid lymphadenopathy; can mimic sarcoidosis and cancer on imaging.

case: 78-year-old woman referred for anemia with elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate, reporting 2 months of lethargy and easy fatigue. Past history: hypertension and hypercholesterolemia, treated with perindopril and atorvastatin. Examination was unremarkable, with no organomegaly or lymphadenopathy; ECOG performance status 1. Blood tests showed hemoglobin 99 g/L, ESR 120 mm/h, mildly elevated creatinine 110 µmol/L, calcium 2.81 mmol/L, and LDH 333 U/L, with normal white cell and platelet counts. Further studies revealed IgG kappa paraprotein 32 g/L, elevated β₂-microglobulin 6.3 mg/L, free kappa light chains 1,400 mg/L with kappa/lambda ratio 280, and urinary Bence-Jones protein (kappa); 24-hour urine protein was normal.

Multiple myeloma (IgG kappa).description: A malignant clonal plasma cell disorder characterized by monoclonal immunoglobulin production and end-organ damage (CRAB features: hypercalcemia, renal impairment, anemia, bone disease).

Smoldering multiple myeloma.description: An asymptomatic clonal plasma cell disorder with higher tumor burden than MGUS but without myeloma-defining events (no CRAB features or biomarkers that mandate therapy).

Monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined si.description: A premalignant plasma cell disorder with low-level monoclonal protein and no end-organ damage attributable to the clone.

AL (light chain) amyloidosis.description: A systemic disease caused by deposition of misfolded immunoglobulin light chains in organs, often arising from a small plasma cell clone.

Light chain cast nephropathy (myeloma ki.description: Renal injury due to intratubular precipitation of excess monoclonal free light chains, typically seen in multiple myeloma and causing acute or subacute kidney dysfunction.

case: 20-year-old male with 3-year history of bilateral breast enlargement without nipple discharge. He reported decreased facial hair growth, small testes, occasional morning erections, blurred vision corrected with glasses, intermittent post-exertional headaches, and a 4-year history of polydipsia and polyuria that had recently improved. Past history included generalized nocturnal tonic-clonic seizures and focal right leg seizures from ages 6–13, treated with carbamazepine until age 14. He also had recent constipation and a chronic pilonidal cyst. Physical examination showed minimal facial hair, bilateral breast enlargement without retraction, masses, or discharge, small testes, a posterior anal fissure, and a small coccygeal lump with central punctum.

Hypothalamic-pituitary lesion (e.g., cra.normalized_text: Hypothalamic-pituitary lesion (e.g., craniopharyngioma or suprasellar germinoma) causing hypogonadism and diabetes insipidus
Hypothalamic-pituitary lesion (e.g., cra.description: A mass in the hypothalamic-pituitary region can disrupt gonadotropin secretion (causing secondary hypogonadism) and impair posterior pituitary function (causing central diabetes insipidus). These tumors often present with headaches and visual symptoms.

Hyperprolactinemia (e.g., pituitary prol.description: Elevated prolactin suppresses GnRH and gonadotropins, leading to hypogonadism with decreased libido/erections, small testes, and sometimes gynecomastia. Larger tumors can cause headaches and visual field defects.

Klinefelter syndrome (47,XXY).description: A common cause of primary testicular failure in males, characterized by small firm testes, gynecomastia, decreased facial/body hair, tall stature, and infertility due to seminiferous tubule dysgenesis with hypergonadotropic hypogonadism.

Primary testicular failure (non-Klinefel.normalized_text: Primary testicular failure (non-Klinefelter; e.g., idiopathic seminiferous tubule failure or prior orchitis)
Primary testicular failure (non-Klinefel.description: Failure of the testes to produce adequate testosterone and sperm leads to hypergonadotropic hypogonadism, manifesting as decreased secondary sexual characteristics, small testes, and sometimes gynecomastia.

hCG-secreting germ cell tumor (testicula.normalized_text: hCG-secreting germ cell tumor (testicular or extragonadal)
hCG-secreting germ cell tumor (testicula.description: Certain germ cell tumors secrete hCG, which increases estrogen production and can cause gynecomastia; they may also suppress gonadotropins leading to hypogonadism. Extragonadal germinomas can arise in the mediastinum or suprasellar region.

case: A 50-year-old man with a history of injecting drug use presented to the emergency department with reduced level of consciousness and left arm weakness following five days of swinging fever, rigors, and headache. His past medical history included hepatitis C infection, paroxysmal atrial fibrillation, and a recent hospital admission for discitis and psoas abscess. On examination, his temperature was 38.4°C but he was hemodynamically stable and alert. Physical findings included a soft early diastolic decrescendo murmur along the left sternal border, splinter hemorrhages, a small digital infarct of the left third toe, and mild upper motor neuron pattern weakness in the left arm. Laboratory investigations revealed normocytic anemia and leukocytosis, with blood cultures growing methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus.

Left-sided infective endocarditis (likel.normalized_text: Left-sided infective endocarditis (likely aortic valve) due to MRSA
Left-sided infective endocarditis (likel.description: Infection of the endocardial surface, commonly involving the aortic valve in left-sided disease. MRSA endocarditis is associated with intravenous drug use and can cause valvular regurgitation and systemic emboli.

Septic embolic ischemic stroke secondary.normalized_text: Septic embolic ischemic stroke secondary to infective endocarditis
Septic embolic ischemic stroke secondary.description: Occlusion of cerebral arteries by infected emboli from cardiac vegetations, leading to ischemic stroke and possible neurologic deficits; commonly arises from left-sided endocarditis.

Brain abscess secondary to hematogenous.normalized_text: Brain abscess secondary to hematogenous spread (MRSA)
Brain abscess secondary to hematogenous.description: Focal intracerebral infection that can result from hematogenous seeding, especially in patients with bacteremia or endocarditis; presents with fever, headache, and focal neurologic deficits.

Bacterial meningitis (MRSA or other bact.normalized_text: Bacterial meningitis (MRSA or other bacterial etiology)
Bacterial meningitis (MRSA or other bact.description: Acute infection of the meninges characterized by fever, headache, and altered mental status; can complicate bacteremia but MRSA meningitis is less common.

Atrial fibrillation-related cardioemboli.description: Thromboembolic ischemic stroke arising from atrial fibrillation-related thrombi, typically presenting with acute focal neurologic deficits.

case: 7-day-old female newborn born at full-term to a G1P1 mother with birth weight of 4,380 gm. Parents denied poor feeding, poor activity, or weak crying. On examination at Day 7, she had normal muscle power, normal reflex, no macroglossia, but slightly decreased facial folds. Newborn screening for Pompe disease showed GAA activity 0.18 uM/h (critical cutoff <0.5) and ratio 42.87 (critical cutoff acid β-glucosidase/GAA ≥20). Laboratory examination revealed elevated pro-BNP (8,738 pg/mL), CK (722 U/L), and ALT (112 U/L). Confirmatory testing showed deficient lymphocyte GAA activity (1.33 nmol/g pro/hr, normal mean 66.7). Patient did not have the common CRIM-positive Taiwan Pompe disease p.D645E variant. Mutation analysis revealed heterozygous c.2024_2026del (p.N675del) and c.2040+1G>T variants in trans.

Classic infantile-onset Pompe disease (G.normalized_text: Classic infantile-onset Pompe disease (Glycogen storage disease type II, acid maltase deficiency)
Classic infantile-onset Pompe disease (G.description: An autosomal recessive lysosomal storage disorder caused by biallelic pathogenic variants in GAA leading to severe deficiency of acid alpha-glucosidase, accumulation of glycogen in cardiac and skeletal muscle, and early-onset cardiomyopathy and muscle weakness.

Late-onset Pompe disease detected by new.normalized_text: Late-onset Pompe disease detected by newborn screening
Late-onset Pompe disease detected by new.description: A milder, variably progressive form of GAA deficiency where skeletal muscle involvement predominates and significant cardiomyopathy is uncommon; often identified via NBS before symptoms.

Danon disease (LAMP2 deficiency).description: An X-linked lysosomal storage disorder due to LAMP2 deficiency, characterized by hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, skeletal myopathy, and variable cognitive involvement; females can present later and more variably than males.

Infant hypertrophic cardiomyopathy of no.normalized_text: Infant hypertrophic cardiomyopathy of non-Pompe etiology (e.g., sarcomeric HCM, RASopathy-associated, or other metabolic cardiomyopathy)
Infant hypertrophic cardiomyopathy of no.description: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy in infancy can arise from sarcomeric gene mutations, RASopathies (e.g., Noonan syndrome), or other metabolic disorders and is often reflected by elevated cardiac biomarkers.

case: 6-year-old girl with a 1-year history of intermittent migratory bone and joint pain, including rib pain, right knee pain with limping, and left flank pain radiating to the left leg. Six days before admission, she developed back pain, worsening limp, and intermittent fever to 39.8°C. The day before admission, she developed periorbital swelling/discoloration, abdominal distention, and periumbilical discoloration. On examination, she was febrile (38.7°C), had bilateral periorbital discoloration, slight limping, flinching with external rotation of the right hip, and a soft, nontender abdomen. Past history included infant gastroesophageal reflux and pollen allergy with allergic rhinitis.

Metastatic neuroblastoma.description: A pediatric neuroendocrine tumor arising from sympathetic neural crest (often adrenal or paraspinal) that commonly metastasizes to bone, bone marrow, and orbits, causing raccoon-eye ecchymoses, bone pain, fever, and abdominal mass/distention.

Acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL).description: A malignant proliferation of lymphoid precursors in bone marrow causing marrow failure and infiltration; common in children and can present with bone/joint pain, fevers, and bruising.

Langerhans cell histiocytosis (LCH).description: A clonal proliferation of Langerhans-type dendritic cells that can involve bone (lytic lesions), skin, and other organs; presents with bone pain, swelling, and sometimes fever.

Ewing sarcoma (with possible metastases).description: A malignant small round blue cell tumor of bone in children/adolescents, often affecting long bones, pelvis, or ribs; can cause bone pain, fever, and limp; metastasis can cause multifocal pain.

Osteomyelitis/septic arthritis.description: Infection of bone or joint causing localized pain, fever, and impaired use; hip involvement causes pain with movement and limp.

Juvenile idiopathic arthritis (JIA).description: A chronic autoimmune arthritis in children characterized by persistent joint inflammation; systemic subtype presents with fevers and rash.

Burkitt lymphoma (abdominal variant).description: An aggressive B-cell non-Hodgkin lymphoma that often presents with rapidly enlarging abdominal masses, fever, and sometimes facial/orbital involvement.

case: 54-year-old woman without comorbidities presented to emergency department with 12-hour history of redness and painful swelling in left gluteal region. Denied trauma. At admission: afebrile (36.2°C), normal blood pressure (109/65 mmHg), heart rate 89 bpm, mild peripheral oxygen desaturation (92% on room air) without respiratory distress. Rest of physical exam normal.

Cellulitis.description: Acute bacterial infection of the dermis and subcutaneous tissue, commonly caused by streptococci or Staphylococcus aureus, presenting with localized erythema, warmth, swelling, and pain.

Cutaneous abscess (gluteal abscess).description: Localized collection of pus within the dermis or subcutaneous tissue, often due to Staphylococcus aureus, presenting with painful, tender, erythematous swelling that may become fluctuant.

Necrotizing soft tissue infection (necro.description: Rapidly progressive infection of fascia and subcutaneous tissues with high mortality, often presenting with severe pain out of proportion, rapidly spreading erythema, edema, and systemic toxicity.

Pyomyositis (gluteal muscle infection).description: Bacterial infection of skeletal muscle, often due to Staphylococcus aureus, leading to deep-seated muscle abscess; may present with localized pain, swelling, and sometimes overlying skin changes, often with fever later.

Hidradenitis suppurativa (gluteal involv.description: Chronic inflammatory disease of hair follicles in intertriginous areas causing painful nodules, abscesses, and sinus tracts; often relapsing and chronic.

Herpes zoster (shingles) involving glute.description: Reactivation of varicella-zoster virus causing a painful, dermatomal rash; may have preceding localized pain and erythema before vesicular eruption.

case: 41-year-old white male with history of myelofibrosis. Past medical history includes splenectomy and allogeneic peripheral hematopoietic stem cell transplantation from single-antigen mismatched unrelated donor 2 years prior. After sun exposure during sailing trip, developed nonpruritic rash on face, trunk and extremities, associated with intermittent fever, muscle pain and weakness. Only current medication is daily oral acyclovir. Vital signs normal. Physical exam showed impaired ability to dorsiflex wrists while bringing palms together ('prayer sign'). Lab results showed: AST 41 U/L, ALT 68 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 147 U/L, total bilirubin 0.7 mg/dL. Antinuclear antibody test positive (1:320) with speckled pattern.

Chronic graft-versus-host disease (cGVHD.normalized_text: Chronic graft-versus-host disease (cGVHD) with cutaneous and musculoskeletal involvement
Chronic graft-versus-host disease (cGVHD.description: Immune-mediated attack by donor lymphocytes on host tissues after allogeneic stem cell transplant, often presenting months to years later with photosensitive or lichenoid/sclerodermoid skin changes, myositis, and possible hepatic involvement.

Dermatomyositis.description: An idiopathic inflammatory myopathy characterized by proximal muscle weakness and characteristic photosensitive cutaneous eruptions; autoantibody-positive in many cases and can show mild transaminase elevation from muscle involvement.

Subacute cutaneous lupus erythematosus (.normalized_text: Subacute cutaneous lupus erythematosus (SCLE) / Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE)
Subacute cutaneous lupus erythematosus (.description: Autoimmune disease with photosensitive rash and positive ANA; SCLE is often limited to skin, while SLE may include systemic features including fevers and myalgias.

Porphyria cutanea tarda (PCT).description: A hepatic porphyria causing photosensitivity with fragile skin and blistering on sun-exposed areas, often associated with liver enzyme abnormalities.

Systemic sclerosis (scleroderma) with ov.description: Autoimmune connective tissue disease characterized by skin thickening and contractures (sclerodactyly) that can impair the 'prayer sign,' sometimes overlapping with inflammatory myopathy.

case: 51-year-old Caucasian male patient with terminal kidney disease presenting with a 10-month history of pruritic papules on sun-exposed areas of extremities. Patient suffered from severe pruritus with impaired sleep. Medical history includes arterial hypertension, hyperuricemia, coronary heart disease, terminal kidney disease due to idiopathic nephropathy, kidney transplants in 1990 and 2001 with rejections in 2000 and 2007, peritoneal dialysis from 2007-2017, ongoing hemodialysis since 2017, and factor V Leiden mutation. No history of habitual UV-light exposure or carcinogen exposure. Medications included felodipine, bisoprolol, clonidine, ramipril, urapidil, cholecalciferol, acetylsalicylic acid, allopurinol, phenprocoumon, thyroxine, iodine, fluvastatin, calcium acetate, omeprazole, and sevelamer carbonate.

Acquired perforating dermatosis (Kyrle d.normalized_text: Acquired perforating dermatosis (Kyrle disease/perforating folliculitis) associated with end-stage renal disease
Acquired perforating dermatosis (Kyrle d.description: A group of perforating disorders seen commonly in patients with chronic kidney disease (and diabetes) characterized by intensely pruritic, umbilicated papules or nodules with a central keratin plug on extensor surfaces; lesions often arise or are exacerbated by scratching (Koebner phenomenon).

Prurigo nodularis secondary to chronic k.normalized_text: Prurigo nodularis secondary to chronic kidney disease (uremic prurigo)
Prurigo nodularis secondary to chronic k.description: A chronic, intensely itchy dermatosis with multiple hyperkeratotic nodules that arises from repeated scratching; commonly associated with systemic pruritic conditions such as chronic kidney disease and can severely impair sleep and quality of life.

Polymorphous (polymorphic) light eruptio.description: A common idiopathic photodermatosis characterized by pruritic papules, papulovesicles, or plaques occurring hours to days after sun exposure on sun-exposed skin, often recurring seasonally.

Photosensitive drug eruption.description: Phototoxic or photoallergic reactions triggered by medications, presenting as pruritic papules, erythema, or eczematous changes confined to sun-exposed areas after UV exposure.

Actinic (photodistributed) lichen planus.description: A variant of lichen planus triggered by sun exposure, presenting with pruritic, flat-topped papules and plaques in sun-exposed areas; more common in spring/summer and in certain skin phototypes.

case: 15-year-old female with a history of ovarian cyst, initially presenting with left arm pain, frontal headaches, and conjunctival hyperaemia without fever or neurological deficits. Seven days later, she developed acute low back pain, left-sided paraesthesia, and left arm weakness. On admission she had mild left-sided weakness, proximal pain in the left arm and leg worsened by movement, normal mental status (GCS 15), no fever, and no meningism. Laboratory tests showed mild leukocytosis and neutrophilia. By day 2, she developed dysuria, urinary retention, worsening left hemiparesis and pain, decreased temperature sensation below T2 on the left and T4 on the right, and bilateral Hoffmann signs. CSF and electromyography were normal.

Acute transverse myelitis (idiopathic/po.description: Inflammatory disorder causing acute to subacute dysfunction of the spinal cord, often following a viral prodrome; can present with pain, sensory level, weakness, and autonomic dysfunction.

Anterior spinal artery syndrome (spinal.normalized_text: Anterior spinal artery syndrome (spinal cord ischemia, e.g., fibrocartilaginous embolism)
Anterior spinal artery syndrome (spinal.description: Ischemic infarction of the anterior two-thirds of the spinal cord, often presenting abruptly with severe back pain, weakness, dissociated sensory loss (pain/temperature), and autonomic dysfunction; can occur in adolescents due to fibrocartilaginous embolism.

Multiple sclerosis (clinically isolated.normalized_text: Multiple sclerosis (clinically isolated syndrome with partial myelitis)
Multiple sclerosis (clinically isolated.description: Immune-mediated demyelinating disease of the central nervous system; in pediatrics, can present with a partial transverse myelitis causing asymmetric weakness and sensory disturbances.

MOG antibody-associated disease (MOGAD).description: An antibody-mediated demyelinating disorder often affecting children; myelitis can be longitudinally extensive, with severe pain, urinary retention, and sometimes normal or mildly abnormal CSF.

Neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder (.description: Autoimmune astrocytopathy characterized by severe, often longitudinally extensive transverse myelitis and/or optic neuritis; can cause marked pain, sensory loss, weakness, and bladder dysfunction.

Spinal epidural abscess (compressive mye.description: Infection in the epidural space causing back pain and progressive cord compression leading to neurologic deficits and bladder dysfunction.

case: 27-year-old male presented with headache, dizziness, nausea, and vomiting for 3 days before admission. Physical examination showed no palpable lymph-node enlargement or hepatosplenomegaly. Laboratory findings showed: WBC count 49.5×109/L, hemoglobin 161 g/L, platelet count 36×109/L, with 95% blasts in peripheral blood smear. Serum lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) was markedly elevated to 13,022 IU/L. Flow cytometry showed leukemic blasts were positive for CD2, CD7, CD5, and CD3, and negative for TdT, CD34, CD13, CD33, CD10, CD19, CD20, and CD22.

T-lymphoblastic leukemia/lymphoma (T-ALL.description: An acute leukemia of immature T-cell precursors that typically presents in adolescents/young adults with high circulating blasts and elevated LDH. Although classically TdT positive, rare cases show TdT negativity while retaining strong T-lineage markers.

T-cell prolymphocytic leukemia (T-PLL).description: An aggressive mature T-cell leukemia of post-thymic T cells characterized by very high leukocyte counts, strong pan–T-cell antigen expression, and TdT negativity. It commonly presents with splenomegaly, lymphadenopathy, and skin involvement, usually in older adults.

Adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma (ATLL, HT.description: A mature T-cell neoplasm driven by HTLV-1 infection, often presenting with leukemic cells expressing mature T markers and TdT negativity. Common features include lymphadenopathy, skin lesions, hypercalcemia, and high LDH; presentations range from indolent to acute leukemic forms.

Hyperleukocytosis with leukostasis secon.normalized_text: Hyperleukocytosis with leukostasis secondary to acute T-lineage leukemia
Hyperleukocytosis with leukostasis secon.description: A life-threatening complication of acute leukemia where very high circulating blast counts increase blood viscosity and impair microvascular perfusion, causing neurologic and respiratory symptoms. Most often seen with acute leukemias and very elevated blast counts.

case: A 36-year-old Chinese man presented with a 1-month history of persistent fever. He was previously healthy with no significant past medical history, specifically no prior TB infections, chronic illnesses, liver or kidney disease, transfusions, malignancy, or immune diseases. He was not taking any regular prescription medications and had not travelled abroad. On admission, vital signs showed temperature 37.2°C, heart rate 119 beats/min, blood pressure 90/48 mmHg, respiration rate 38 breaths/min with oxygen saturation 88%. Physical examination revealed an acutely ill appearance and pulmonary rales in both lungs. He presented with persistent fever, pancytopenia, and hyperferritinemia with clinical deterioration including acute respiratory failure.

Hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (HLH).description: A life-threatening hyperinflammatory syndrome due to uncontrolled immune activation, often triggered by infections (e.g., EBV, TB), malignancy, or autoimmune disease; characterized by persistent fever, cytopenias, organ dysfunction, and markedly elevated ferritin.

Severe community-acquired pneumonia with.description: A severe lower respiratory tract infection leading to hypoxemic respiratory failure and systemic inflammatory response; ARDS can develop with diffuse alveolar damage and severe hypoxemia.

Miliary tuberculosis.description: Disseminated Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection with hematogenous spread causing systemic symptoms and multi-organ involvement; can cause persistent fever, cytopenias, and respiratory compromise.

Adult-onset Still's disease (AOSD) with.normalized_text: Adult-onset Still's disease (AOSD) with possible macrophage activation syndrome
Adult-onset Still's disease (AOSD) with.description: An autoinflammatory disorder characterized by high spiking fevers, arthralgia, rash, and very high ferritin; can evolve into macrophage activation syndrome (a form of HLH) causing cytopenias and organ failure.

Acute leukemia (e.g., AML/ALL) with seco.normalized_text: Acute leukemia (e.g., AML/ALL) with secondary infection
Acute leukemia (e.g., AML/ALL) with seco.description: A malignant proliferation of immature hematopoietic cells causing marrow failure (pancytopenia) and infection-related complications; can present with fever and systemic illness.

Sepsis of unknown origin with multiorgan.normalized_text: Sepsis of unknown origin with multiorgan dysfunction
Sepsis of unknown origin with multiorgan.description: A dysregulated host response to infection leading to life-threatening organ dysfunction and shock; can cause respiratory failure, hypotension, and laboratory abnormalities including cytopenias and elevated ferritin.

COVID-19 pneumonia with hyperinflammator.description: SARS-CoV-2 infection causing viral pneumonia and hypoxemic respiratory failure; severe cases can feature a hyperinflammatory state with elevated ferritin and hematologic abnormalities.

case: An 81-year-old man presented to the ICU 10 days after a 4-week cruise in New Caledonia, Vanuatu, the Solomon Islands, and New Zealand. He was reported to have been in perfect health during the cruise. On examination, he was febrile (39.1°C) and comatose with a Glasgow Coma Scale score of 6. He exhibited hemiplegia of the left side, paresis of the right upper limb, normal tendon reflexes, and a Babinski sign on the left side. A transient rash was observed within 48 hours of admission. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis showed leukocyte count of 41/mm³ (98% polymorphonuclear leukocytes), protein level of 76 mg/dL, and CSF:blood glucose ratio of 0.75.

Dengue-associated encephalitis/encephalo.description: Neurologic complications of dengue infection, which can include encephalitis or encephalopathy, occur during or shortly after acute dengue. They are more likely in older adults and can present with fever, altered consciousness, seizures, and focal deficits. Dengue is endemic in many South Pacific islands.

Japanese encephalitis (arboviral encepha.description: A mosquito-borne flavivirus prevalent in parts of Asia-Pacific that causes encephalitis with fever, rapidly progressive altered mental status, seizures, and focal neurologic deficits; mortality and neurologic sequelae are high in older adults.

Herpes simplex virus (HSV-1) encephaliti.description: A leading cause of sporadic fatal encephalitis in adults, characterized by fever, altered consciousness, focal neurologic signs, and seizures, often with temporal lobe involvement. CSF typically shows elevated protein and pleocytosis; early neutrophilic predominance can occur, with normal glucose.

Listeria monocytogenes meningoencephalit.description: A foodborne bacterial infection that frequently affects older adults and can cause meningoencephalitis with fever, altered mental status, and focal neurologic deficits. CSF may show neutrophilic pleocytosis and elevated protein, with glucose that may be normal or mildly decreased.

Cerebral malaria (Plasmodium falciparum).description: A severe complication of falciparum malaria characterized by impaired consciousness or coma and sometimes focal neurologic signs. It can occur in travelers to malaria-endemic regions and often presents with high fever. CSF may be relatively unremarkable or show mild pleocytosis and protein elevation.

case: 20-year-old man with Crohn’s disease diagnosed at age 10, previously treated with prolonged glucocorticoids and improved on weekly adalimumab over the past 3 years. Presented with 3 weeks of upper respiratory symptoms (sore throat, nonproductive cough, rhinorrhea, chills), followed 2 weeks before presentation by cramping left calf pain and swelling that progressed to the foot, with a purpuric/erythematous rash on the dorsum of both feet. Exam showed left ankle synovitis, intact nasal septum, normal peripheral pulses, and discomfort from left leg pain.

IgA vasculitis (Henoch–Schönlein purpura.description: An IgA-mediated small-vessel vasculitis often triggered by upper respiratory infections, characterized by palpable purpura on the lower extremities, arthralgias/arthritis, and potential gastrointestinal or renal involvement.

Cutaneous leukocytoclastic vasculitis (h.normalized_text: Cutaneous leukocytoclastic vasculitis (hypersensitivity vasculitis), possibly anti-TNF–induced
Cutaneous leukocytoclastic vasculitis (h.description: Immune complex–mediated small-vessel vasculitis of the skin that presents with palpable purpura, often triggered by infections or medications (including TNF inhibitors like adalimumab) and may include arthralgia/arthritis.

Deep vein thrombosis (DVT) of the left l.normalized_text: Deep vein thrombosis (DVT) of the left lower extremity
Deep vein thrombosis (DVT) of the left l.description: Formation of a blood clot in a deep vein, commonly presenting with unilateral calf pain and swelling; inflammatory bowel disease is a known hypercoagulable risk state.

ANCA-associated small-vessel vasculitis.description: A necrotizing small-vessel vasculitis that can present with palpable purpura, arthralgias, and systemic symptoms; often involves kidneys and lungs, and may be preceded by constitutional or upper airway symptoms.

Erythema nodosum (Crohn’s-related extrai.description: A panniculitis associated with inflammatory bowel disease that presents with tender erythematous nodules on the shins and can be accompanied by arthralgia/arthritis.

case: A 47-year-old man presented to his primary care physician with a six-month history of left-sided sore throat, ipsilateral otalgia, and a six-week history of a left-sided neck mass. He had never smoked and drank less than 5 units of alcohol per week. On examination in the ENT clinic, a firm fixed lymph node was palpable in the upper anterior triangle.

HPV-associated oropharyngeal squamous ce.normalized_text: HPV-associated oropharyngeal squamous cell carcinoma (tonsil/base of tongue)
HPV-associated oropharyngeal squamous ce.description: A malignancy of the oropharynx, often arising from the palatine tonsil or base of tongue. Frequently HPV-positive, it commonly presents in non-smokers with unilateral sore throat, referred ear pain, and metastatic cervical lymphadenopathy.

Nasopharyngeal carcinoma.description: An Epstein–Barr virus–associated carcinoma arising in the nasopharynx. It often presents with painless cervical lymphadenopathy and can cause referred ear symptoms and throat discomfort.

Metastatic squamous cell carcinoma to ce.normalized_text: Metastatic squamous cell carcinoma to cervical lymph node from occult head and neck primary
Metastatic squamous cell carcinoma to ce.description: Cervical nodal metastasis from an as-yet unidentified primary tumor in the upper aerodigestive tract; common sites include the oropharynx, hypopharynx, or larynx.

Non-Hodgkin lymphoma involving cervical.normalized_text: Non-Hodgkin lymphoma involving cervical lymph nodes
Non-Hodgkin lymphoma involving cervical.description: A malignant lymphoid neoplasm that can present with painless, firm lymphadenopathy in the cervical region; systemic B symptoms may or may not be present.

Tuberculous cervical lymphadenitis (scro.description: Mycobacterial infection of cervical lymph nodes leading to chronic lymphadenopathy; nodes can be firm and may become matted or fluctuant over time.

case: 72-year-old white woman with 10-year history of recurrent cystitis. No systemic symptoms. Physical exam showed slight anemia. Urine cultures were positive for Escherichia coli. No hepatosplenomegaly or lymphadenopathy detected by CT and ultrasound. Esophagogastroduodenoscopy and subsequent biopsies were negative for both pathologic lymphoid infiltrate and Helicobacter pylori. Otolaryngologic examination and bone marrow biopsy were negative. Serology for hepatitis C virus and hepatitis B virus was negative. No monoclonal component found in serum protein electrophoresis.

Recurrent uncomplicated urinary tract in.normalized_text: Recurrent uncomplicated urinary tract infections due to postmenopausal urogenital atrophy
Recurrent uncomplicated urinary tract in.description: Estrogen deficiency after menopause leads to atrophic changes in the vaginal and urethral mucosa, altered vaginal microbiota, and decreased local immunity, predisposing to recurrent bacterial cystitis.

Diabetes mellitus predisposing to recurr.normalized_text: Diabetes mellitus predisposing to recurrent urinary tract infections
Diabetes mellitus predisposing to recurr.description: Chronic hyperglycemia impairs host defenses and promotes glycosuria, fostering bacterial growth and recurrent UTIs, particularly with Enterobacterales such as E. coli.

Pelvic organ prolapse with incomplete bl.normalized_text: Pelvic organ prolapse with incomplete bladder emptying (cystocele) leading to recurrent UTIs
